# 66.28 Biblical Record: 2 Peter 1:20 — Origin of Prophecy, Not a Ban on Reading

2 Peter 1:20–21 has already been controlled as production-doctrine:

> “Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation. For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.”

Chapter 30 established the text as inspiration-doctrine: men spoke from God as carried by the Holy Spirit. Chapter 57 used it as production of a non-failing record: prophecy of Scripture is not of private unloosing and not brought by human will as ultimate source. The present file does not retry those files. It uses the text to refuse a misuse that would destroy this chapter’s definition of interpretation.

The misuse says:

> **No prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation; therefore readers may not interpret; therefore stating sense is forbidden; therefore Nehemiah 8:8 is a crime.**

The misuse fails the paragraph’s own next sentence. Verse 21 gives the reason: the prophecy came not by the will of man; men spoke as moved by the Holy Ghost. The “for” locates the claim in origin, not in a ban on later readers. ἐπίλυσις (*epilusis*, G1955), already handled in this manuscript as unloosing of prophetic origin, is the production-term, not a later prohibition of giving the sense. Private unloosing names how prophecy did not come. It does not name a later rule that the writings may not be understood.

The misuse would also contradict the letter’s own next movement. 2 Peter 3:16 names wresting of writings that include things hard to be understood. Hardness and wresting are unintelligible if stating sense is forbidden. Forbidden sense-giving would make wresting and faithful reading equally impossible. The letter does not write that impossibility.

The present file therefore holds two sentences together. Prophecy of Scripture is not of private unloosing as to origin (Chapters 30, 57, used not retried). Readers may and must state sense as later act, accountable to writings that already stand (Nehemiah 8:8; Acts 17:11; Luke 24:45). Those sentences are compatible. They are not rivals. Collapse of verse 20 into a ban on interpretation is transfer’s opposite error: not the reader becoming the writing, but the writing becoming unreadable in order to protect the writing. The writings do not require that protection.

Thus:

> **2 Peter 1:20 warrants origin-doctrine already earned: prophecy is not of private unloosing. It does not ban later accountable sense-giving. Production and interpretation remain two operations.**

# 66.29 Biblical Record: 1 Corinthians 4:6 — Not Above That Which Is Written

1 Corinthians 4:6 locates later claims about teachers under a written ceiling:

> “And these things, brethren, I have in a figure transferred to myself and to Apollos for your sakes; that ye might learn in us not to think of men above that which is written, that no one of you be puffed up for one against another.”

The surrounding argument is party-claim: Paul, Apollos, Cephas, and the rest treated as rival heads (1 Corinthians 1–4). The present file does not rewrite those chapters as a church-order file. It takes the ceiling as it stands. “That which is written” is the measure. Thinking of men is the later act. The later act is not to rise above the writing.

Two objects are again on the page. The writing stands as the limit of later speech about men. Interpreters, teachers, and party-heads remain men. Transfer would raise a favourite teacher above the writing by using the writing as a banner. The sentence forbids that rise. Despair would hear the sentence as if the writing could not govern later speech about teachers. The sentence exists because the writing does govern that speech.

What the verse does not do here is become Chapter 68’s system-file or Chapter 69’s displacement-file. Party-spirit as a later pathology remains later. The present force is the ceiling: later claims about men, including claims made by quoting, remain under that which is written.

Thus:

> **1 Corinthians 4:6 warrants the distinction: that which is written is the ceiling of later speech about men. Teachers remain under the writing. A party-claim that rises above the writing has claimed the second object as if it were the first.**

# 66.30 Biblical Record: Galatians 1:8–9 — Even an Apostle Judged by the Deposit

Galatians 1:8–9 binds the highest later claim to the gospel already received:

> “But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed. As we said before, so say I now again, If any man preach any other gospel unto you than that ye have received, let him be accursed.”

Chapter 53 already used the paragraph as a test of later title-claims. Chapter 57 already used it as evidence that the writings distinguish the deposit from later enlargement. The present use is distinction. The gospel already preached and received is one object. A later preaching, even from “we” or from an angel from heaven, is another. The later preaching is judged by the deposit. The deposit is not judged by the later preacher’s standing.

If authority of interpretation migrated from the writing — or from the apostolic deposit as already given — into the later mouth by the act of preaching, the paragraph would be impossible. An apostle’s later contrary mouth would be as authoritative as his former mouth. An angel’s later mouth would be as authoritative as the received gospel. The text curses that migration. Standing of the speaker does not create standing of a contrary sense.

The paragraph also refuses despair. “That which we have preached” and “that ye have received” are identifiable. Another gospel is identifiable as other. Identifiability is communication. The deposit can be known well enough to detect a rival. Detection is not a second Graphē. It is the deposit functioning as measure.

What the paragraph does not do here is become Chapter 71’s accepted-heresies file, and it does not become a finished account of Galatian controversy as history beyond the text. The present force is the ranking of objects: deposit first; later mouth second, even when the later mouth is an apostle or an angel.

Thus:

> **Galatians 1:8–9 warrants the distinction at its sharpest: the already-given deposit measures later speech, including later speech from the highest later mouths. Office does not transfer. An angel does not transfer.**

# 66.31 Biblical Record: Mark 7 and Matthew 15 — Tradition as Rival Claim

Mark 7:6–13 and Matthew 15:3–9 record the commandment of God set aside by a later claim presented as tradition.

Mark 7:8–9, 13:

> “For laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men… Full well ye reject the commandment of God, that ye may keep your own tradition… Making the word of God of none effect through your tradition, which ye have delivered: and many such like things do ye.”

Chapter 58 already named Mark 7 as a reason the synthesis refuses interpreter-infallibility by institutional location. The present use is distinction, not Chapter 68’s system-file, and not Chapter 69’s displacement-file. Two objects are on the page. The commandment of God, the word of God, is one. The tradition of men, delivered and held, is another. The later claim is presented as a way of honouring God. The verdict is that the later claim lays aside, rejects, and makes of none effect the word.

The passage exhibits what this chapter must already refuse: a later statement of how to live under God that claims the writing’s field while evacuating the writing. That is authority of interpretation asserted as if it were authority of Scripture. The word remains the word. The tradition remains a later claim. Making the word of none effect is the later claim’s work, not the word’s failure.

What the passage does not do here is finish the analysis of tradition as a system, of institution as institution, or of secondary sources becoming primary. Those are Chapters 68–69. The present force is the two objects exhibited as two, and the later object refused as a court above the word. Unverifiable reconstructions of later rabbinic offices beyond what the record states are not used as premises.

Thus:

> **Mark 7 and Matthew 15 warrant the distinction as a live conflict in the record: the word of God and the tradition of men are two; the later claim may evacuate the word while quoting the field of the word; the word remains the measure of the claim. The system-file remains later.**

# 66.32 Reconstructing the Aletheia Proposition: Graphē as Premiere Convention, Not Interpreter as Graphē

A reconstructible proposition from the project’s own doctrinal materials states that true experience in conformity with Christ pillows in the unleavened sincerity and truth of the Graphē — Holy Writ as writings of unchallenged standing — whether for persons, organizations, governments, or nations; that this writing is the premiere convention for hearing from God; and that absence of sound judgment and presence of unskillfulness are responsible for later aridity, tergiversation, and accepted heresies among persons and organizations that claim the name.

The proposition is not adopted as “the source says.” It is tested.

**What is claimed.** Experience that is truly in conformity with Christ is governed by the Graphē’s truth, not by a substitute that will not sit under the writing. The premiere convention is the writing. Later unskillfulness is a later failure of persons and organizations, not a failure of the convention.

**What the claim means.** “Pillows in” names dependence and rest: the experience takes its measure from the writing. “Premiere convention” names the writing as first among conventions for hearing. Persons and organizations are not excluded from the measure by being large. They are not included in the writing’s standing by being large.

**Premises.** The Graphē is the primary written authority (Chapter 65). The record does not fail as what it actually communicates (Chapter 57). God is true; every man is a liar (Romans 3:4, used above). Human accounts about God are to be tested (Chapter 14).

**Biblical correspondence.** John 10:35; John 17:17; John 8:31–32; 1 Thessalonians 2:13; Isaiah 8:20; Romans 3:4; 2 Peter 3:16. The correspondence holds for the present distinction: the convention is the writing; the later person or organization remains a later speaker.

**What follows.** The proposition coheres with the distinction: if the Graphē is the premiere convention, the interpreter is not the premiere convention. Organizations that claim the name remain under the writing. Labels are not the measure.

**What does not follow here.** That *apeiros*, tergiversation, accepted heresies, and aridity have been examined as dedicated files. That *spoudazō* has been examined. That the First Principles have been taught. That every later practice calling itself Christian is thereby certified. Those remain later or already refused.

Thus:

> **The reconstructible proposition is received as coherence with the distinction, not as a substitute for the join, and not as Chapters 70–73 or the First Principles written now. The premiere convention is the Graphē. The interpreter is not the Graphē.**

# 66.33 Reconstructing the Bible-Introduction Proposition: Notes About the Writing Are Not the Writing

A reconstructible proposition from the Bible Introduction materials states that the Bible is God’s inspired revelation-record, not an amulet that works by mere presence; that its teachings are to be studied and practiced; that “all Scripture,” not a part, is given by inspiration of God; that the reader is invited to see for himself what related passages are actually saying; that novel interpretations and theories supported by personal opinion alone are to be laid aside; and that the notes and comments gathered around the text are helps toward the writing, not the writing.

The proposition is not adopted as “the source says.” It is tested.

**What is claimed.** The writing is revelation-record and will, to be used as such, not as a charm. Later notes are later speech about the writing. The reader’s work is to see what the passages say. Personal opinion is not the measure.

**Premises already in force.** Chapters 15–22 defined the Bible and the Graphē. Chapters 30–31 established inspiration and “all.” Chapter 57 established non-failure as record. Chapter 65 established primary written authority. The present chapter has defined interpretation as accountable sense-giving.

**What follows for the distinction.** A writing that is revelation-record, not a charm, is used as measure by being read and tested, not by being possessed as an object. Notes about the writing are interpretation in the defined sense: later statements of sense. They may be true as correspondence. They do not inherit the writing’s standing by being printed beside it. The Introduction’s invitation to see for oneself what related passages say is coherence with Acts 17:11, not a second gate.

**What does not follow here.** That every later note in a study edition is therefore false. That literal sense, already a methodological preference in those materials, has been rewritten as this file’s complete hermeneutic. That “Christ never interpreted” — if offered as a sweeping historical claim beyond the texts — has been adopted as a ban on stating sense. Nehemiah 8:8 and Luke 24:27 refuse that ban. Movement X remains the labour-file. Chapter 67 remains the species-file.

Thus:

> **The reconstructible Introduction proposition is received as coherence: the writing is measure by what it is; notes about the writing are not the writing; personal opinion is not the court. Helps remain helps.**

# 66.34 Distinctions Required by the Conclusion

The conclusion requires distinctions already named as objects and now stated as required by the verdict.

**This chapter is not a second gate.** Chapter 65 remains the gate-file. The present file uses the gate as the first object. Using is not rewriting.

**This chapter is not a catalog of specific misreadings.** Chapter 67 remains the species-file. The present file exhibits that readings can fail. Exhibiting the possibility is not cataloguing the species.

**This chapter is not a treatment of theology, philosophy, tradition, and institution as systems.** Chapter 68 remains the system-file. Mark 7 has been used as exhibition of two objects in conflict, not as that later analysis.

**This chapter is not a finished account of secondary sources becoming primary.** Chapter 69 remains the displacement-file. Naming two objects is not tracing the displacement.

**This chapter is not Chapters 70–73, Movement X, or the First Principles.** Pathology, labour, and entry remain later.

**Understanding is not authority over the text.** A correct reading remains under the writing.

**Quotation is not the writing.** A cited sentence in a later mouth is a later use.

**Community claim is still a claim.** Number of speakers does not convert later speech into the Graphē.

**2 Peter 1:20 is origin, not a ban on sense-giving.** Production and interpretation remain two operations.

A further distinction belongs with them because the word “authority” invites it:

**Derivative force of a correct reading is not a second Graphē.** Correspondence has force as correspondence. It does not have force as replacement.

Thus:

> **The distinctions are the verdict’s shape. They prevent the opening of Movement IX from becoming a second gate, a premature catalog, a system-file, a displacement-file, a ban on reading, or a baptism of readers.**

# 66.39 Competing Claim: Scripture Is Authoritative, Therefore My Reading Is

The reduction says:

> **The Graphē is the primary written authority. I read the Graphē. Therefore my reading is the primary written authority. To deny this is to deny Scripture.**

The reduction fails.

The premise is the gate. The conclusion is transfer. The inference does not follow. Authority of the measure is not authority of the measurement. Chapter 57 already refused the analogue for infallibility. Chapter 65 already refused to confer the gate upon every later quotation. The present file has now named the inference as Movement IX’s first live failure.

The biblical record refuses the reduction in several mouths at once. “Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures” is spoken to possessors and users of the writings. Wresting is named of unlearned and unstable readers of writings that already stand. The Bereans are noble for testing a sermon, not for becoming the sermon’s equal as court. Galatians 1 curses a later contrary mouth even when the mouth is “we” or an angel. Mark 7 judges a tradition that occupies the field of the word while laying the word aside. Romans 3:4 ranks God as true and every man as a liar. Those sentences are unintelligible as a baptism of later readings.

The reduction often presents itself as a defence of Scripture. The defence is the attack. If my reading is the gate, the gate is no longer the Graphē. It is my reading. The writing has been replaced by a later claim that uses the writing’s name. That replacement is the confusion this chapter exists to refuse.

The reduction’s official form does not rescue it. “The church reads; therefore the church’s reading is the gate” is the same inference with a larger subject. Chapter 57 already refused infallibility of the church as a transfer from the record. Chapter 52 already refused later vote as origin of the corpus. Number and office do not create a valid inference from a writing’s standing to a later mouth’s standing.

Thus:

> **“Scripture is authoritative, therefore my reading is” fails. The gate remains the writing’s. The reading remains a reading. Defence of Scripture that baptizes the reader is not defence of Scripture.**

# 66.40 Competing Claim: All Readings Are Equal Because Readers Err

The reduction says:

> **Readers are fallible. Therefore no reading may be judged as true or false of the writing. All readings are equal. Distinction of text from interpretation is the abolition of knowledge. To deny this is arrogance.**

The reduction fails.

The premise is the reader’s fallibility, which this chapter affirms. The conclusion is equality of readings and the abolition of the writing as court. The inference does not follow. Fallibility of the measurer is not equality of measurements, and it is not failure of the line.

The biblical record refuses the reduction in several mouths at once. Nehemiah 8:8 records sense given and understanding caused. Luke 24 records understanding opened toward writings that already stood. Acts 17:11 records a search whether those things were so — a search that has a “whether,” not a “never.” Matthew 22:29 names error as error, not as one more equal reading. 2 Peter 3:16 names wresting as wresting, unto destruction, not as a legitimate alternative sense. Galatians 1 names another gospel as another, and curses it. Those sentences are unintelligible if all readings are equal.

The reduction often presents itself as humility. The humility is a claim of immunity. If no reading may be judged, the reader is safe from the writing. Safety from the writing is not humility before the writing. It is the second object claiming the right not to appear before the first.

The reduction’s pious form does not rescue it. “We are only interpreters” is true as a denial of transfer. It is false as a denial of correspondence. Interpreters may correspond. Interpreters may fail to correspond. Both possibilities require a writing that communicates and that remains the court.

Thus:

> **“All readings are equal because readers err” fails. Fallibility is affirmed. Equality is denied. The writing remains able to judge readings. Humility that abolishes the court is not humility.**

# 66.41 Competing Claim: This Chapter as Already Chapters 67–73

The reduction says:

> **Once the two authorities have been distinguished, Movement IX is finished. Write the catalog now, write the systems now, write the displacement now, write the pathologies now. The later chapters are surplus.**

The reduction fails.

Chapter 65 already refused the same collapse when it was offered as “the gate is already mishandling.” This chapter refuses the remaining half of that collapse’s first step: the distinction is not already the catalog, the systems, the displacement, or the pathologies.

Without dedicated later files, the book would possess two named objects and still lack the earned examination of how readings fail, how systems replace the text, how secondary sources take the primary seat, how turning aside works, how heresies become accepted, how reasonability dries, and how the reader is *apeiros*. Those examinations are the next necessary questions. Naming them is not performing them.

Thus:

> **This chapter is not already Chapters 67–73. The distinction is the distinction. Later questions remain later.**
