# 66.42 Reason Through the Evidence

The inference can now be exhibited.

**Premise 1.** The Graphē is the primary written authority by which truth is known, tested, reasoned through, taught, discerned, and lived — the decisive written measure among written authorities (Chapter 65, used not retried).

**Premise 2.** Scripture, as inspired authenticated corpus, is an infallible record: it does not fail as truthful divine writing of what it actually communicates; that verdict attaches to the writing, not to the interpreter (Chapter 57, used not retried).

**Premise 3.** Authority of the written Word is not infallibility of interpreters; God true, every man a liar, remains the ranking (Chapter 58; Romans 3:4, used not retried as a second ontology-file).

**Premise 4.** Interpretation is the later act of stating what the writing means; that act is real, accountable, and not the writing (definition at this stage; Nehemiah 8:8; Luke 24:45).

**Premise 5.** The writings themselves exhibit later speech judged by the writing, and exhibit later speech failing while the writing stands: ye do err, not knowing the scriptures; wresting unto destruction; searching whether those things were so; searching without coming; not above that which is written; even an apostle or an angel judged by the deposit; the commandment laid aside by tradition (Matthew 22:29; 2 Peter 3:16; Acts 17:11; John 5:39–40; 1 Corinthians 4:6; Galatians 1:8–9; Mark 7).

**Premise 6.** Truth is not sincerity, not popularity, not institutional consensus; the thing described is not the description of the thing; later speech about the word is not the word (Chapters 1–3, 14, 65, used not retried).

**Inference.** Therefore the authority of Scripture and the authority of interpretation are two objects. The writing’s standing does not transfer automatically to a reader’s or community’s claim about what the text means. Fallibility of the reader is compatible with infallibility of the record. An authoritative truthful text does not make every interpretation of it authoritative. The fact that readers err does not make all readings equal. A correct reading has derivative force as correspondence; it does not become a second Graphē. An incorrect reading remains incorrect; it does not become the writing by quoting, by occupying an office, or by gathering a community. The investigator is warranted, with full force, in receiving this as Movement IX’s first word. Chapter 67 remains the next question.

**Alternative explanations refused.** That Scripture’s authority baptizes the reader’s reading. That all readings are equal because readers err. That this file is already Chapters 67–73. That this file is Chapter 65 retried or Chapter 57 rewritten. That 2 Peter 1:20 bans stating sense. That distinction abolishes knowledge. Those alternatives fail the join, the biblical record of two objects, and the premises already in force.

Thus:

> **The inference is inspectable. The distinction follows from the conjunction of the gate, the record’s non-failure, the ranking of God and man, the definition of interpretation as later act, and the writings’ own exhibitions. The alternatives fail as accounts of that conjunction.**

---

# 66.43 Explicit Versus Inferred

**Explicit.** Let God be true, but every man a liar. Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of God. Some things hard to be understood, which the unlearned and unstable wrest, as they do also the other scriptures, unto their own destruction. They searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so. They read in the book distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading. He opened their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures. Search the scriptures; they are they which testify of me; and ye will not come to me. No prophecy of the scripture is of any private unloosing; prophecy came not by the will of man; men spoke as moved by the Holy Ghost. Not to think of men above that which is written. Though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel than that ye have received, let him be accursed. Laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men; making the word of God of none effect through your tradition.

**Inferred, as warranted.** That “authority of Scripture” and “authority of interpretation” name two objects. That the Graphē’s standing does not transfer automatically to a later statement of sense. That fallibility of the reader is compatible with infallibility of the record. That an authoritative truthful text does not make every interpretation authoritative. That the fact that readers err does not make all readings equal. That a correct reading’s force is derivative correspondence, not a second Graphē. That 2 Peter 1:20, controlled as origin, does not ban later accountable sense-giving. That Movement IX is open as assigned.

**Not inferred here.** Chapter 67’s catalog of species. Chapter 68’s system-analysis. Chapter 69’s displacement-file. Chapters 70–73 as finished pathologies. Movement X’s labour-files. *Spoudazō* as this file’s object. *Apeiros* as this file’s object. The Six First Principles as content. Physical indestructibility of every later copy. Infallibility of every interpreter. A reconstructed council inventing official senses. Unverifiable imprimatur-offices as if they were in the text. A ban on stating sense. Equality of all readings.

The line is the difference between a distinction-file and a later-file. Crossing it would be theft. Refusing to infer what the conjunction warrants would be under-claim. The chapter has inferred what the conjunction warrants. It has not inferred what later premises must still supply as species, systems, displacement, pathology, and labour.

Thus:

> **What is explicit has been distinguished from what is inferred. Later doctrines have not been inferred here. The warranted inferences about two objects, failed reductions, and the opening of Movement IX have been drawn.**

---

# 66.44 The Warranted Conclusion Stated with Full Force

The investigator is warranted, with full force, in receiving this conclusion:

> **The authority of Scripture and the authority of interpretation are two objects. The Graphē’s standing as primary written authority does not transfer automatically to a reader’s or community’s claim about what the text means.**

An authoritative truthful text does not make every interpretation of it authoritative. The fallibility of the interpreter is compatible with the infallibility of the record. The fact that readers err does not make all readings equal.

The warrant is the conjunction already named. The Graphē is the primary written authority (Chapter 65). The record does not fail as truthful divine writing of what it actually communicates, and that verdict attaches to the writing, not to the reader (Chapter 57). God is true; every man is a liar (Romans 3:4). Interpretation is a later act of stating sense, real and accountable, not the writing. The writings themselves exhibit later speech judged by the writing, and exhibit later speech failing while the writing stands. Therefore the two authorities must remain distinct.

A correct reading states what the writing communicates. It has force as correspondence. It does not become a second Graphē. An incorrect reading remains incorrect. It does not become the writing by quoting the writing, by occupying an office, by gathering a community, or by pleading humility.

Competing reductions fail. “Scripture is authoritative, therefore my reading is” fails the gate, the ranking, and the record. “All readings are equal because readers err” fails the record’s naming of error, wresting, another gospel, and nobility of testing. This chapter as already Chapters 67–73 fails the locked assignments.

The investigator is therefore warranted, with full force, in receiving Movement IX’s first word as drawn. The distinction is in force. Sequence continues. Sequence is not hesitation.

Thus:

> **The authority of the text is not the fallibility of the interpreter, and it is not the standing of the interpreter’s claim. The conclusion is the conjunction of members already earned, exhibited in the record’s own two-object grammar, and fenced against the live reductions. Movement IX is open.**

---

# 66.45 The Scope of This Stage

The scope of this stage is the distinction between the Graphē’s standing and the standing claimed for a later statement of sense. The scope is not the later catalog of how readings fail, not the later analysis of systems, not the later tracing of displacement, and not the later labour of rightly handling the writing.

What belongs inside the scope has been done. The two objects have been defined. The surrounding objects have been distinguished. The premises have been used and not retried. The limits have been located once as the shape of the doctrine. Authority of Scripture, interpretation, and authority of interpretation have been defined. Why the two must remain distinct has been stated. Transfer and despair have been named. The four members of positive warrant have been joined. The biblical record of two objects has been exhibited. The required distinctions have been stated. The live reductions have been refused. The inference has been shown. The explicit has been distinguished from the inferred. The conclusion has been stated with full force.

What belongs outside the scope has been named once and left. How Scripture is misread remains Chapter 67. Systems remain Chapter 68. Displacement remains Chapter 69. Pathologies remain Chapters 70–73. Labour remains Movement X. The First Principles remain later. *Spoudazō* remains a dedicated later chapter. Species of error have been exhibited as live, not catalogued as finished. Tradition has been exhibited as a rival claim in Mark 7, not examined as a system.

The four governing questions have not been conflated. The ontological question — what the two objects are — has been answered as writing and later claim. The epistemological question — how the distinction is known — has been answered by the conjunction of members already earned and by the writings’ own exhibitions, not by a circle from a favourite reading to itself. The evidential question — what warrants refusing transfer and despair — has been answered by the join, the record, and the failure of the reductions. The hermeneutical question of how the authoritative text is correctly understood remains later as labour and as species. The present file has opened that question by distinguishing the text’s standing from the interpreter’s standing. It has not pretended to be Chapter 67 or Chapter 84.

Thus:

> **The scope is the distinction. The distinction is complete at this level. Later scopes remain later because they are different questions.**

---

# 66.46 Apply the Standard

The governing authorial maxim remains:

> **Do not merely tell the reader what to conclude.**
>
> **Give the reader the definitions, evidence, biblical record, reasoning, distinctions, and inferential steps necessary to see why the conclusion follows.**

And:

> **Do not make the reader choose between reason and Scripture. Teach the reader to reason through Scripture.**

This chapter has defined authority of Scripture as the Graphē’s already-earned standing as primary written measure, interpretation as the later act of stating sense, and authority of interpretation as the standing claimed for that later act. It has distinguished those objects from a second gate, from Chapter 57 rewritten, from Chapter 58 rewritten, from a catalog of misreadings, from system-files, from a displacement-file, from later pathologies, from Movement X, and from the First Principles. It has used premises already in force and refused premises that remain later. It has given one clean account of sequence and limits. It has named transfer and despair as the two live failures. It has stated the positive warrant as conjunction. It has exhibited the biblical record of two objects. It has refused the live reductions. It has distinguished the explicit from the inferred.

The Easton test has been applied in its proper analogue. A later writer may say that Scripture’s authority baptizes the authorized reader, or that all readings are equal because readers err, or that 2 Peter 1:20 forbids stating sense, or that this distinction is already the catalog and already the systems, or that notes printed beside the text inherit the text’s standing, or that a community’s consensus is the writing’s living voice. The manuscript has not accepted those sentences as premises. It has asked what the writing is, what the preceding argument has earned, and what the record actually warrants.

Circularity has been refused. The argument is not: my reading is Scripture because I read Scripture; therefore interpreters and traditions are infallible; therefore the movement is finished. The argument is: the writing is the primary written authority; the record does not fail as record; God is true and every man a liar; interpretation is a later act; the writings exhibit later speech judged by the writing; therefore the two authorities are two.

Prematurity has been refused. The chapter has not consumed Chapters 67–73, Movement X, or the First Principles.

Duplication has been refused. The gate remains Chapter 65. Infallibility of the record remains Chapter 57. The synthesis remains Chapter 58. The John 10 arc remains Chapters 59–63. The identification remains Chapter 64. Lexical establishment remains Chapters 20–22. Truth’s definition remains Chapters 1–3. God’s truthfulness remains Chapters 10–12. Human accounts remain Chapter 14. The present function is the dedicated distinction, and the opening the locked guidance names.

Source-integration has been performed without “the source says.” The reconstructible proposition that experience in conformity with Christ is governed by the Graphē as premiere convention has been tested as coherence with the distinction. The reconstructible Introduction proposition that the writing is revelation-record rather than charm, and that notes about the writing are not the writing, has been tested as coherence with two objects. Neither has been treated as a licence, and neither has been treated as Chapters 67–73 or the First Principles.

Thus:

> **The standard has been applied: the authority of Scripture has been distinguished from the authority of interpretation as Movement IX’s first word, not announced as a slogan, and not postponed as if the distinction were weak.**

---

# 66.47 From Distinction to How Scripture Is Misread

A distinction, now controlled as two objects that must not be collapsed, still leaves a further question.

The distinction-file is in force. The authority of Scripture and the authority of interpretation are two. The Graphē’s standing does not transfer automatically to a later claim about what the writing means. Fallibility of the reader is compatible with infallibility of the record. Those sentences are the cleared ground. They are not yet the dedicated examination of how the later act fails: how Scripture is misread through poor perception, deficient understanding, faulty inference, context failure, or improper handling of the text.

If the distinction were not named, the next question would still be how the authority of the text is to be held apart from the fallibility of the interpreter. The distinction has been named. If this chapter were already that later examination, the next file would be repetition. This chapter is not that later examination. The next question is therefore the construction the locked assignment names: How Scripture Is Misread.

That is the proper open of the next chapter. The distinction was never meant to be a slogan that finishes Movement IX, and it was never meant to baptize every later reading or to equalize all readings. It was meant to be the naming of two objects as two, sufficient to justify taking the next question, which is the question two named objects themselves force once they have been named: how does the later act fail in the ways the writings and the locked assignment require us to examine?

The next file must not steal this distinction as if two objects had not been named. This file must not steal that catalog as if Chapter 67 were already written. Naming the neighbourhood is not performing the examination.

---

# What Has Been Established

This chapter has established:

1. **Authority of Scripture versus authority of interpretation, in this argument, is the dedicated distinction of two objects — the Graphē’s standing as primary written authority, and the standing claimed for a later statement of what the writing means — not a motto, not a second gate, and not a catalog of species.**
2. **Authority of Scripture at this stage is the Graphē’s already-earned standing as primary written measure — used, not retried.**
3. **Interpretation at this stage is the later accountable act of stating the writing’s sense — not the writing, not a licence, not a despair.**
4. **Authority of interpretation at this stage is the standing claimed for that later act — named as a claim, not granted as a second Graphē.**
5. **The two must remain distinct because they are two, because the gate is otherwise a blank check, because mishandling is otherwise unintelligible, and because communication is otherwise denied.**
6. **Transfer fails: “Scripture is authoritative, therefore my reading is” is an invalid inference. Detectability of error is not automatic correctness.**
7. **Despair fails: “all readings are equal because readers err” is an invalid inference. Fallibility of the reader does not migrate into the writing.**
8. **Fallibility of the reader is compatible with infallibility of the record. The writing’s non-failure is not the reader’s. The reader’s failure is not the writing’s.**
9. **Understanding is not authority over the text. A correct reading sits under the writing.**
10. **Quotation is not the writing. Quotation can convey knowledge and is not, by itself, understanding.**
11. **A community’s claim about the writing is still a claim. Consensus is not the Graphē.**
12. **Positive warrant, first member: the gate does not transfer. Primary written authority remains the writing’s rank.**
13. **Positive warrant, second member: the record does not fail; the reader may. Two objects, not one, and not none.**
14. **Positive warrant, third member: God true, every man a liar. The writing is received on the first side; the interpreter remains on the second side as interpreter.**
15. **Positive warrant, fourth member: the writing is court of later speech. Sense-giving appears before that court; it does not become that court.**
16. **Romans 3:4 warrants the ranking the distinction requires.**
17. **Matthew 22:29 warrants that writings already in hand can be unknown; possession is not knowledge; error is not the writings’ failure.**
18. **2 Peter 3:16 warrants that writings that stand can be wrested; wresting is the readers’ destruction; hardness is not the abolition of sense.**
19. **Acts 17:11 warrants that later speech is tested by the writings; nobility is assigned to the testing.**
20. **Nehemiah 8:8 warrants treating interpretation as a real accountable act toward a writing that remains the object.**
21. **Luke 24:25–27, 44–45 warrant that writings already stand; hearers may be slow; understanding may be opened toward those writings without replacing them.**
22. **John 5:39–40 warrant that searching is not the writings; use may fail; standing does not fail with the use.**
23. **2 Peter 1:20, controlled as origin, does not ban later accountable sense-giving. Production and interpretation remain two operations.**
24. **1 Corinthians 4:6 warrants that which is written as the ceiling of later speech about men.**
25. **Galatians 1:8–9 warrant that the already-given deposit measures later speech, including later speech from the highest later mouths.**
26. **Mark 7 and Matthew 15 warrant the word of God and the tradition of men as two; the system-file remains later.**
27. **The reconstructible Aletheia proposition that the Graphē is the premiere convention is tested as coherence with the distinction, not as “the source says,” and not as Chapters 70–73.**
28. **The reconstructible Introduction proposition that notes about the writing are not the writing is tested as coherence with two objects. Helps remain helps.**
29. **The conclusion’s required distinctions include: this chapter ≠ a second gate; ≠ Chapter 67; ≠ Chapter 68; ≠ Chapter 69; ≠ Chapters 70–73, Movement X, or the First Principles; understanding ≠ authority over the text; quotation ≠ the writing; community claim ≠ the Graphē; derivative force ≠ a second Graphē.**
30. **What is explicit has been distinguished from what is inferred, and later doctrines have not been inferred here.**
31. **“Scripture is authoritative, therefore my reading is” fails.**
32. **“All readings are equal because readers err” fails.**
33. **Treating this chapter as already Chapters 67–73 fails.**
34. **The distinction attaches to two objects. It does not confer the writing’s standing upon every later quotation, tradition, impression, institution, or reader. God true, man fallible, remains the ranking.**
35. **This chapter opens Movement IX because its assigned word has been stated.**
36. **This chapter opens Chapter 67 by naming the next necessary question without answering it.**
37. **What is reserved is Chapter 67; Chapters 68–73; entire Movement X (Chapters 74–85); the First Principles themselves; and σπουδάζω (*spoudazō*) as a dedicated chapter.**

---

# Chapter Summary

> **The chapter’s central conclusion:** The authority of Scripture and the authority of interpretation are two objects. Because the Graphē is the primary written authority already earned; because the record does not fail as truthful divine writing of what it actually communicates, and that verdict attaches to the writing, not to the reader; because God is true and every man a liar; because interpretation is a later act of stating sense, real and accountable, not the writing; and because the writings themselves exhibit later speech judged by the writing, and exhibit later speech failing while the writing stands — the writing’s standing does not transfer automatically to a reader’s or community’s claim about what the text means. An authoritative truthful text does not make every interpretation of it authoritative. Fallibility of the reader is compatible with infallibility of the record. The fact that readers err does not make all readings equal. A correct reading has derivative force as correspondence; it is not a second Graphē. Competing reductions fail: “Scripture is authoritative, therefore my reading is”; “all readings are equal because readers err”; this chapter as already Chapters 67–73. The investigator is warranted, with full force, in receiving this as Movement IX’s first word. The distinction is in force. Chapter 67 remains later because it is a later question. Movement IX is open.

The essential architecture is:

> **Gate-file already stated → two authorities defined → objects distinguished → premises used, not retried → one clean account of sequence and limits → authority of Scripture, interpretation, and authority of interpretation defined → why the two must remain distinct → transfer and despair named → four members joined → biblical record of two objects → distinctions stated → reductions refused → distinction warranted → Movement IX opened → sequence to how Scripture is misread.**

The governing distinctions are:

- **The distinction** is not **a second gate.**
- **This file** is not **Chapter 57 or Chapter 58 rewritten.**
- **Authority of Scripture** is not **authority of interpretation.**
- **The writing’s standing** is not **the interpreter’s standing.**
- **Understanding** is not **authority over the text.**
- **Quotation** is not **the writing.**
- **A community’s claim** is not **the Graphē.**
- **A correct reading’s force** is not **a second Graphē.**
- **Fallibility of the reader** is not **failure of the record.**
- **Infallibility of the record** is not **infallibility of the reader.**
- **2 Peter 1:20 as origin** is not **a ban on stating sense.**
- **This file** is not **Chapter 67, Chapter 68, Chapter 69, or Chapters 70–73.**
- **This file** is not **Movement X or the First Principles.**
- **Using Chapters 57, 58, and 65** is not **reprinting them.**
- **Limits** are **the shape of the doctrine**, not **delayed doubt.**
- **Sequence** is **not hesitation about this level.**

The decisive principle is:

> **Distinguish the authority of the text from the fallibility of the interpreter, claiming what the conjunction warrants and not more: the Graphē’s standing does not transfer automatically to a later claim about what the writing means — an authoritative truthful text does not make every interpretation authoritative, and the fact that readers err does not make all readings equal — before examining how Scripture is misread. Draw the conclusion the premises support. Do not draw the conclusions that still require later premises. Then ask how Scripture is misread.**

---

# Transition to Chapter 67

Movement IX is open. Its first word has been stated.

The Graphē has been shown to be the primary written authority by which truth is known, tested, reasoned through, taught, discerned, and lived. The writing is the decisive written measure. That gate is in force. The authority of that writing has now been distinguished from the authority claimed for a later statement of what the writing means. The writing’s standing does not transfer automatically to the interpreter. Fallibility of the reader is compatible with infallibility of the record. An authoritative truthful text does not make every interpretation of it authoritative. The fact that readers err does not make all readings equal. Transfer fails. Despair fails. Movement IX’s first word is in force.

The writings that present that distinction do not leave unused the further question of the ways the later act fails. Two objects have been named as two. Named objects still leave the dedicated examination of how the second object errs: poor perception, deficient understanding, faulty inference, context failure, improper handling of the text. The next necessary question is therefore not a new curiosity. It is the question the locked assignment names:

> **How is Scripture misread, now that the authority of the text has been distinguished from the fallibility of the interpreter, and now that the next file’s first word is to be that catalog of failure rather than a second distinction, and rather than a finished system-file?**

That is the subject of:

# Chapter 67 — How Scripture Is Misread

> **Examine errors arising from poor perception, deficient understanding, faulty inference, context failure, or improper handling of the text.**

The investigation now moves from:

> **the authority of Scripture versus the authority of interpretation**
>
> to:
>
> **how Scripture is misread.**

# End of Chapter 66

chapters.title: How Scripture Is Misread
chapters.body:
> **Movement IX — When Authoritative Truth Is Mishandled**

> **Central objective:** Examine how Scripture is misread — errors arising from poor perception, deficient understanding, faulty inference, context failure, or improper handling of the text — so that the later act of stating sense is shown to fail in inspectable modes, not as a mystery of an obscure writing, and not as a licence that every later claim about the writing is as good as every other. This continues Movement IX. It uses Chapter 66’s distinction. It is not a second distinction-file, not a treatment of theology, philosophy, tradition, and institution as systems, not a finished account of secondary sources becoming primary, and not Chapters 70–73, Movement X, or the First Principles written in advance.

---

## Chapter Assignment

Chapter 66 established Movement IX’s first word. The authority of Scripture and the authority of interpretation are two objects. The Graphē stands as the primary written authority already earned. A reader’s or community’s claim about what that writing means is a later act of stating sense. The writing’s standing does not transfer automatically to that later act. Fallibility of the reader is compatible with infallibility of the record. An authoritative truthful text does not make every interpretation of it authoritative. The fact that readers err does not make all readings equal. The distinction-file is in force.

Chapter 66 ended by naming the next necessary question, not a new curiosity:

> **How is Scripture misread, now that the authority of the text has been distinguished from the fallibility of the interpreter, and now that the next file’s first word is to be that catalog of failure rather than a second distinction, and rather than a finished system-file?**

That is this chapter’s assignment.

The locked Table of Contents states the work in one sentence:

> **Examine errors arising from poor perception, deficient understanding, faulty inference, context failure, or improper handling of the text.**

The locked knowledge-flow places this examination after the distinction of authorities and before the dedicated examination of theology, philosophy, tradition, and institution as systems. Two objects have been named as two. Named objects still leave the dedicated account of how the second object fails. Naming that a measuring-line is not a measurement is not yet examining how measurements go wrong. The present file is that examination, at the level the premises warrant, and not beyond it.

The present file does not re-draw the distinction of Chapter 66. It cites that distinction as established. It does not re-prove that the Graphē is the primary written authority. It cites Chapter 65 as established. It does not re-answer why the record does not fail as truthful divine writing of what it actually communicates. It cites Chapter 57 as established. It does not treat theology, philosophy, tradition, and institution as finished systems. It does not write Chapter 68. It does not finish the account of secondary sources becoming primary. It does not write Chapter 69. It does not write tergiversation, accepted heresies, aridity, or *apeiros* as dedicated files. It does not write Movement X. It does not enter the First Principles. It examines the modes of misreading without which Movement IX would possess two named objects and still lack the first earned account of how the later act fails.

A ranked writing, now distinguished from the later claim that states its sense, still leaves a further question. If the later act can fail, how does it fail? If the failure is only a mood, the catalog is a slogan. If the failure is every later question Movement IX and Movement X will ask, the investigation has stopped reasoning. The present file is the modes, at the level the writings and the locked assignment require, and not beyond it.

The remaining question of the book’s sequence follows. Sequence continues the investigation. It does not convert the present line into hesitation.

---

## Central Objective

> **To examine, from the biblical record and from premises already in force, how Scripture is misread, so that Movement IX’s second word is one inspectable verdict: the later act of stating sense fails in named modes — poor perception, deficient understanding, faulty inference, context failure, and improper handling — while the writing remains the measure of those failures; to keep this catalog distinct from a treatment of secondary systems, from a finished displacement-file, and from the later pathology-files and labour-files; to refuse the reductions that say the writing is at fault because readers fail, that say sincerity baptizes a reading, that say spiritualizing is the higher method, that say one isolated useful sentence suffices, or that treat this chapter as already Chapters 68–73 or Movement X; and to refuse both under-claim and over-claim.**

The governing movement is:

> **Distinction-file already stated → question of how the later act fails → misreading defined at this stage → five modes defined → objects distinguished → premises already in force used, not retried → one clean account of sequence and limits → positive warrant from communication, from the writings’ own diagnoses, and from the remaining possibility of a correct reading → each mode examined with biblical record → reconstructible Introduction and Aletheia propositions tested as coherence → competing reductions refused → inspectable inference → warranted conclusion → sequence to systems beside the Graphē.**

The chapter’s conclusion is affirmative:

> **Scripture is misread when the later act of stating sense fails to correspond to what the writing actually communicates. That failure is not one mood. It is a set of inspectable operations: poor perception, deficient understanding, faulty inference, context failure, and improper handling. The writing remains the measure of those operations. The writing is not made obscure by being mishandled, and the mishandling is not made true by being sincere, useful, spiritualized, isolated, official, or frequently repeated. A correct reading remains possible because the writing communicates. An incorrect reading remains incorrect because the writing communicates. This continues Movement IX. It is not Chapter 66 retried. It is not Chapters 68–73. It is not Movement X. That is this chapter’s conclusion, stated here with full force.**

The remaining questions follow by sequence. The verdict is already in force as warranted catalog, not as postponed guesswork.

---

# 67.1 The Question Created by the Preceding Chapter

Movement IX is open. Its first word has been stated. The Graphē is the primary written authority by which truth is known, tested, reasoned through, taught, discerned, and lived. That gate is in force. The authority of that writing has been distinguished from the authority claimed for a later statement of what the writing means. The writing’s standing does not transfer automatically to the interpreter. Fallibility of the reader is compatible with infallibility of the record. An authoritative truthful text does not make every interpretation of it authoritative. The fact that readers err does not make all readings equal. Transfer fails. Despair fails. The distinction-file is in force.

Chapter 66 established the distinction. That conclusion is a premise here. Two objects still leave a further question: if the later act of stating sense can fail while the writing stands, how does that act fail? Distinction names the possibility of failure. The present file examines the modes.

A people can receive the distinction as a piety — “we are only interpreters” — and still not have examined how interpretation goes wrong. They can quote Matthew 22:29 as a proverb and still not have asked what “not knowing” is as an operation. They can quote 2 Peter 3:16 as a warning and still not have asked what wresting is as a handling. The writings themselves force the further analysis. He has said they err, not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of God. He has asked whether they do not yet perceive, whether they have eyes and see not. He has named hearing without understanding. He has opened writings that already stood to hearers who were slow of heart. An apostle has named writings that stand being wrested unto destruction. A tempter has cited what is written and omitted what the cited writing required. The first distortion of a spoken command already added, subtracted, and reversed. Those sentences, already neighbouring the distinction, have a joint consequence concerning modes. If they have none, “how Scripture is misread” is a title. If they have every consequence a later slogan wishes — systems examined now, displacement finished now, *apeiros* written now, *spoudazō* written now — the investigation has stopped reasoning.

The question is therefore not:

> **How is the authority of Scripture to be distinguished from the authority of interpretation?**

That question has been answered.

The question is:

> **How is Scripture misread — by what inspectable operations of poor perception, deficient understanding, faulty inference, context failure, and improper handling — now that the two authorities have been distinguished, and not as a second distinction, and not as a finished system-file?**

If Movement IX proceeded from the distinction to theology as a system without examining modes, it would skip the locked step. If it treated this file as already Chapter 66, it would convert a species-file into a second distinction-file. If it treated this file as already Chapters 68–73, it would close the movement’s later questions inside its second word. The present file is the dedicated examination of how Scripture is misread.

That is a different operation from piety. It is the operation this chapter must perform.

---

# 67.2 What This Chapter Does Not Repeat

Chapters 1–3 established truth as conformity to reality, distinct from belief, popularity, institutional consensus, and sincerity as a determinant of truth. Those conclusions remain premises. This chapter does not re-write the opening ontology of truth. It uses truth as already defined, now as the object a reading may or may not state.

Chapters 4–7 established knowledge, evidence, reason, and rational warrant as inspectable operations. Those conclusions remain premises. This chapter does not re-write the opening epistemology. It uses perception, inference, and judgment as already defined, now as the operations whose failure is misreading.

Chapters 10–12 established that God is the ground of truth and that falsehood is incompatible with Him. Chapter 14 established that human accounts about God are themselves to be tested. Those conclusions remain premises. This chapter does not re-write them. It uses them: a failed reading is a failed human account of a writing that participates in God’s truthfulness as record.

Chapters 20–22 established γραφή (*graphē*, G1124) as writing that, in biblical usage, designates Holy Writ / Scripture. Those conclusions remain premises. This chapter does not re-try the lexical files. It uses them: the object being misread is that writing.

Chapters 56–57 established inspiration’s guarantees and why the record does not fail as truthful divine writing of what it actually communicates, including speaker-distinction. Those conclusions remain premises. This chapter does not re-try the infallibility-file. It uses speaker-distinction as a rule against one live mode of mishandling.

Chapter 65 established the Graphē as the primary written authority. Chapter 66 distinguished that standing from the standing claimed for a later statement of sense. Those conclusions remain premises. This chapter does not re-try the gate or the distinction. It uses them as the ranked object and the later act now examined in its failures.

This chapter does not recatalogue Romans 3:4, Acts 17:11, Nehemiah 8:8, or 1 Corinthians 4:6 as if the distinction of two objects were still in doubt. It may use those passages as already-earned court and contrast. The new function is this:

> **To examine how the later act fails in the five modes the locked assignment names; to refuse both emptiness and overclaim; and to leave the system-files, the displacement-file, the later Movement IX pathologies, labour, and the First Principles in their assigned files.**

---

# 67.3 Define the Question: How Scripture Is Misread

**How Scripture is misread**, in this chapter, is the dedicated account of the later act of stating sense failing to correspond to what the Graphē actually communicates, examined as inspectable modes rather than as a single mood of “error.”

The phrase is easily abused. In ordinary speech “misreading” may mean any disagreement, any difficulty, any later application, any refusal of a school’s official sense, any admission that a passage is hard, or the entire later investigation of systems, displacement, heresy, aridity, and unskillfulness. None of those senses is this chapter’s object.

Four elements belong to the definition.

First, **failure of correspondence**. Misreading is not the existence of a later act. Chapter 66 already established that stating sense is a real accountable act. Misreading is that act failing of its object: the sense stated is not the sense communicated.

Second, **modes, not one fog**. The locked assignment names five operations: poor perception, deficient understanding, faulty inference, context failure, improper handling. Those operations may combine. They are still distinguishable. A catalog that names only “people err” has not examined how.

Third, **the writing as measure of the failure**. The writing is not rewritten by being misread. Chapter 52 already established that wresting does not unmake standing. Chapter 66 already established compatibility of a fallible reader with a non-failing record. The present definition inherits both: misreading is the reader’s failure of a stable object.

Fourth, **not those other claims**. The definition excludes, as not this object: a retry of Chapter 66; a treatment of theology, philosophy, tradition, and institution as systems; a finished account of secondary sources becoming primary; tergiversation, accepted heresies, aridity, and *apeiros* as finished files; Movement X’s labour-files; the First Principles as this file’s achievement. Those exclusions are part of the definition. They are not a later apology.

Thus:

> **The question of this chapter is not whether text and interpretation are two, why the Graphē is the primary written authority, or how later systems replace the text. Those questions have been examined or remain later. The question is how Scripture is misread in the modes just named.**

---

# 67.4 Distinguish Objects That Must Not Be Collapsed

The investigation fails at the first step if it treats different objects as one.

**This catalog and Chapter 66’s distinction.** This chapter examines how the later act fails. Chapter 66 named the later act as distinct from the writing. Distinction and catalog neighbour one another. They are not the same file. To treat this file as Chapter 66 retried would hide the modes inside a second distinction. To omit the modes in order to protect the distinction would leave the distinction unjoined to the second word Movement IX assigns.

**Misreading and difficulty.** A passage may be hard to be understood and still not be misread. 2 Peter 3:16 names both hardness and wresting. Hardness is a feature of some writings. Wresting is a handling of those writings. To collapse the two is to baptize wresting as difficulty, or to treat every difficulty as already a crime.

**Misreading and disagreement.** Two readers may disagree, and one or both may be misreading, or the disagreement may still be a labour toward a sense not yet settled. Disagreement is a social fact. Misreading is a failure of correspondence. The first does not, by existing, prove the second of every party.

**The five modes and one another.** Poor perception is not yet deficient understanding, though it yields it. Deficient understanding is not yet faulty inference, though it invites it. Faulty inference is not yet context failure, though isolation often produces it. Context failure is not yet improper handling as a completed wresting, though it is already a mishandling of neighbours. The catalog is a distinction of operations, not a claim that a failed reading uses only one.

**This chapter and later files.** Systems, displacement, tergiversation, accepted heresies, aridity, *apeiros*, scholarly labour, *spoudazō*, and the First Principles remain later. A mode may appear in a later system. Appearance is not those files written now.

Thus:

> **Misreading is failure of correspondence in named modes. It is not the distinction retried, not mere difficulty, not mere disagreement, not one undifferentiated fog, and not the later files under another name.**

---

# 67.5 Premises That May Be Used, and Premises That May Not

The chapter may use, as already in force:

- Truth as conformity to reality, distinct from belief, popularity, institutional consensus, and sincerity as a determinant of truth (Chapters 1–3).
- Knowledge, evidence, reason, comparison, inference, and rational warrant as inspectable operations (Chapters 4–7).
- God as the ground of truth, truthful, faithful, immutable, and incapable of falsehood (Chapters 10–12).
- Human accounts about God as themselves to be tested (Chapter 14).
- γραφή as writing that, in biblical usage, designates Holy Writ / Scripture (Chapters 20–22).
- Inspiration of Scripture as writing; “all Scripture”; inspiration’s guarantees, including speaker-distinction (Chapters 30–31, 56).
- Infallibility of the record as not infallibility of the interpreter (Chapter 57).
- The Graphē as the primary written authority (Chapter 65).
- Authority of Scripture as distinct from authority of interpretation; transfer and despair already refused (Chapter 66).
- Biblical exhibitions already used as two objects in conflict: Matthew 22:29; 2 Peter 3:16; Luke 24; John 5:39–40; Mark 7 / Matthew 15; Acts 17:11; Nehemiah 8:8 — used now as mode-evidence, not as a second distinction-file.

The chapter may not use, as if already finished:

- Chapter 68’s treatment of theology, philosophy, tradition, and institution as systems, except so far as a mode must already be exhibited when a later claim occupies the field of the word.
- Chapter 69’s finished account of secondary sources becoming primary.
- Chapters 70–73 as finished pathology-files; *apeiros* as a dedicated object; aridity as a dedicated object; tergiversation as a dedicated object; accepted heresies as a dedicated object.
- Movement X’s labour-files; *spoudazō* as a dedicated object; rightly dividing as a finished file; quotation, meaning, and knowledge as a finished dedicated distinction; readiness for the Six First Principles as this chapter’s achievement.
- The Six First Principles themselves as content established here.
- Unverifiable historical colour offered as a premise: a reconstructed school that invented allegory as a world-system, a named extra-biblical imprimatur-office as if it were in the text, weather, crowd-size, or architectural invention beyond what the record states.

The chapter may use neighbouring passages that exhibit modes of failed reading. It may not treat those passages as a substitute for the join of the preceding argument, and it may not treat Chapters 68–73 or Movement X as already performed.

Thus:

> **Premises already in force may be used as members of the catalog. Premises that remain later may not be used as if finished. The modes are the present object.**

---

# 67.6 The Sequence of Levels: One Clean Scope Section

What this chapter does not settle is a matter of sequence, not of doubt about what it does settle.

The investigation proceeds by levels. Each level answers its question with full force. The next level remains next because it is a different question.

**Already in force.** Truth is conformity to reality. God is the ground of truth and cannot lie. Revelation has been given and authenticated. Scripture as writing is God-breathed. The record does not fail as truthful divine writing of what it actually communicates. The Graphē is the primary written authority. The authority of that writing has been distinguished from the authority claimed for a later statement of sense. Transfer fails. Despair fails. Fallibility of the reader is compatible with infallibility of the record.

**This level.** Given those premises, Scripture is misread when the later act fails of what the writing communicates, and that failure occurs in inspectable modes: poor perception, deficient understanding, faulty inference, context failure, and improper handling. The warrant is full at this level. It is not postponed until Chapter 68 in order to keep the present catalog weak, and it is not inflated into a system-file, a displacement-file, a pathology-file, or a labour-file in order to make the catalog sound larger than modes of a failed reading.

**Next levels, named once.** Theology, philosophy, tradition, and institution as systems belong to Chapter 68. Secondary sources becoming primary belongs to Chapter 69. Tergiversation, accepted heresies, aridity, and *apeiros* belong to Chapters 70–73. Scholarly labour, perception as a dedicated stage-file, reasoning through the Word as a labour-file, quotation and knowledge as a dedicated file, *spoudazō*, exercise, maturity, rightly dividing, and readiness for the Six First Principles belong to Movement X. Those files remain later.

**Limits that belong to this level itself, not to later hesitation.** This catalog is not a second distinction-file. This catalog is not a denial that a correct reading can be had. This catalog is not a grant that all readings are equal. This catalog is not a system-file. This catalog is not a displacement-file. Using Chapters 57, 65, and 66 is not rewriting them. Difficulty is not already wresting. Disagreement is not already proof of misreading in every party. Those limits are part of what the species-file is. They are not a stack of clauses designed to drain the positive conclusion.

The chapter will therefore state the positive warrant with full force, locate the limits as belonging to the doctrine rather than as apologies, and name later files once as later files. It will not repeat, under every paragraph, that the present conclusion is not proof of a later conclusion. Sequence is already the account of that difference.

Thus:

> **The present catalog is in force at this level. Later verdicts remain later because they are different questions. Limits named here are the shape of the doctrine, not a delayed doubt about the doctrine.**

---

# 67.7 Define “Misreading” at This Stage

**Misreading**, in this argument, is the later act of stating the Graphē’s sense in a way that does not correspond to what that writing actually communicates.

Four notes belong to the definition at this stage.

First, **an act with an object**. The object is the writing’s communication. Chapter 57 attached non-failure to what the writing actually communicates, not to every later inference drawn from it. Misreading is failure of that attachment on the reader’s side.

Second, **detectable in principle**. Chapter 66 already used the analogue: an infallible measuring-line does not make every measurement correct; it makes incorrect measurement detectable in principle. Detectability is not automatic detection. It is the reason a catalog of modes is possible. If failure were undetectable, “how Scripture is misread” would name a fog.

Third, **possible without malice, and possible with it**. A reader may fail by dullness, haste, isolation, or invalid inference without intending to corrupt. A reader may also handle the word deceitfully. The catalog includes both. Intention distinguishes culpability. It does not create a second definition of correspondence.

Fourth, **not the writing’s failure**. The Sadducees’ error in Matthew 22 does not unmake Exodus 3. The wresting in 2 Peter 3:16 does not unmake Paul’s epistles or the other scriptures. The first distortion in Genesis 3 does not unmake the command that was given. Misreading leaves the object standing.

Thus:

> **Misreading, at this stage, is failed correspondence of a later statement of sense to the writing’s communication. It is not difficulty as such, not disagreement as such, not the writing’s collapse, and not yet the later files.**

---

# 67.8 Define the Five Modes Named by the Locked Assignment

The locked assignment does not name a mood. It names five operations. They must be defined before they are used as premises.

**Poor perception** is failure at the first intake of what is there: eyes that do not see what the writing presents, ears that do not hear what it says, attention that does not register the words, the relations, or the fact that a thing has been said. Mark 8:17–18 names the operation: “perceive ye not yet, neither understand? have ye your heart yet hardened? Having eyes, see ye not? and having ears, hear ye not? and do ye not remember?” Perception here is not a later mystical faculty. It is the first reception of what is present.

**Deficient understanding** is failure to grasp the sense of what has been perceived or could have been perceived. Words may be in hand. The sense is not. Matthew 22:29 names the operation as not knowing the scriptures. Acts 8:30 names it as a question: “Understandest thou what thou readest?” Understanding is not a second writing. It is reception of the writing’s sense.

**Faulty inference** is failure in the movement from what the writing says to a conclusion it does not warrant. The text used may be genuine. The step is invalid. Matthew 16:6–12 exhibits disciples concluding “bread” from “leaven.” Matthew 4:6 exhibits a citation of Psalm 91 used to warrant a leap the psalm does not command. Inference is already defined in Chapters 5–6. Faulty inference in this file is that operation performed upon Scripture.

**Context failure** is failure to keep a statement among its neighbours: speaker, audience, occasion, surrounding argument, wording, genre, and the other scriptures that bear upon the same subject. Isolation is the typical form. A sentence is treated as if it had no before and after, no speaker, and no corpus. Context is not a later academic fashion. It is the writing’s own location of its sentences.

**Improper handling** is the completed misuse of the writing as writing: wresting, corrupting, handling deceitfully, changing a literal communication into a second meaning the text does not give, treating figurative language as if it conveyed no literal truth, or using the writing to evacuate the writing. 2 Peter 3:16 names wresting. 2 Corinthians 2:17 and 4:2 name corrupting and deceitful handling. Improper handling may include the other four modes as its materials. It is named separately because it is the writing used against its own communication.

The five may occur together. A hardened heart may refuse to perceive, and therefore not understand, and therefore infer badly, and therefore isolate a sentence, and therefore wrest. Naming five is not claiming five sealed compartments. It is refusing to leave failure as one fog.

Thus:

> **The five modes are operations: intake, grasp, inference, location, and use. They are the catalog’s species. They are not yet systems, displacement, or the labour-files.**

---

# 67.9 Why Modes Matter: Failure Is Operational, Not Mystical

The catalog exists because failure is operational.

If misreading were a fate, the writings’ rebukes would be unintelligible. “Ye do err” names an act that should not have been done. “Perceive ye not yet” names an operation that should have been performed. “Understandest thou what thou readest?” names a question that can receive a yes. “Which they … wrest” names a handling. Fate does not wrest. An operation does.

If misreading were a mystery of an obscure book, the writings’ simplicity-claims and their hardness-claims would be collapsed into one fog. The Bible Introduction materials will be tested below as the proposition that the writing is given to be understood, and that the ordinary reasons it is not understood are willful operations, not a defect in the Giver. That proposition must be tested, not adopted as a slogan. It already names why modes matter: if the writing communicates, failure is on the receiving operations.

If misreading were only institutional, the catalog would already be Chapter 68. Persons misread. Organizations misread. The operation is the same in kind: a later act failing of a writing. The speaker’s size does not create a new mode. It may later create a system. That is a later question.

Modes matter because they can be examined. Perception can be asked: what is on the page? Understanding can be asked: what does that communicate? Inference can be asked: does this conclusion follow? Context can be asked: who speaks, to whom, in what argument, among which neighbours? Handling can be asked: is the writing being used as what it is, or used to evacuate what it is? Those questions are the reason this chapter is an investigation and not a lament.

Thus:

> **Modes matter because failure is an operation of the later act. The writing remains the object. The operations remain inspectable. Mystery is not the doctrine. Fate is not the doctrine.**

---

# 67.10 Positive Warrant: The Writing Communicates; Failure Is the Later Act

The first member of the positive warrant is communication already in force.

Because the God who cannot lie has made known, because all Scripture is God-breathed as writing, because inspiration’s guarantees attach to what the writing actually communicates, and because the Father’s word has been identified as truth, the Graphē is a communicating writing. A communicating writing can be received. It can also be failed of. Failure of a communicating writing is not the writing’s silence. It is the later act’s miss.

Chapter 66 already refused despair on this ground: if distinction meant that no later statement can correspond, the writing would have failed as communication. The present member uses the same ground from the other side: if the writing communicates, a later statement can fail of that communication, and the failure can be named. Communication is the reason both a correct reading and a misreading are intelligible.

The first member also locates blame without writing the later pathology-files. The writing is not an amulet that works by mere presence. The reconstructible Introduction proposition that the Bible is not a charm, but a revelation-record to be studied and practiced, coheres here as warrant: presence of a copy is not reception of the communication. Reception can fail. The copy remains a copy of a communicating writing.

Thus:

> **The first member is communication. The writing speaks as writing. Misreading is the later act’s failure of that speech, not the speech’s collapse into silence.**

---

# 67.11 Positive Warrant: The Writings Themselves Diagnose Modes

The second member of the positive warrant is the writings’ own diagnoses.

The Graphē does not leave mishandling as an extra-biblical worry. It names error as not knowing the scriptures. It names perception refused. It names hearing without understanding. It names wresting. It names corrupting the word. It names handling the word deceitfully. It names making the word of God of none effect. It names a citation of what is written used to warrant what the written thing does not command. It names a first distortion that questions, adds, and reverses a given command. Those are not later chapter-titles imported into the text. They are the text’s own account of failed later acts.

The second member is why the catalog is not a theory imposed upon a silent Bible. Chapter 7 already established that the writings invite reason. Chapter 61 already established that Christ reasons from what is written. The present file uses that already-earned fact in a new function: the writings also reason about failed reading. They do not only supply material to be read. They diagnose the reading.

The diagnoses are modes, not yet systems. “Not knowing the scriptures” is deficient understanding. “See ye not” is poor perception. “They reasoned among themselves” toward a false conclusion is faulty inference. A citation cut from its neighbours is context failure. “Wrest” and “corrupt” and “deceitfully” are improper handling. The writings supply the species. The present file arranges them as the locked assignment requires.

Thus:

> **The second member is the writings’ own diagnoses. The catalog is read out of the record, not lowered onto it as a later scheme.**

---

# 67.12 Positive Warrant: Correct Reading Remains Possible

The third member of the positive warrant is the remaining possibility of a correct reading.

A catalog of failure that implied the impossibility of success would be despair under another name. Chapter 66 already refused that despair. The present file must refuse it as a misuse of the catalog. The existence of poor perception does not abolish perception. The existence of wresting does not abolish a sense that can be violated. Nehemiah 8:8 already recorded sense given and understanding caused. Luke 24 already recorded understanding opened toward writings that already stood. Acts 17:11 already recorded a search whether those things were so. Acts 8 already recorded a reading that did not yet understand, and then a sense given from the same writing. Those sentences remain premises. They are the catalog’s necessary counterpart: modes of failure are intelligible because modes of reception are real.

The third member is also why the catalog is worth writing. If no correct reading can be had, examining how readings fail is theatre. If a correct reading can be had, examining how readings fail is labour toward the writing. Movement X will examine that labour as dedicated files. The present member only states what the catalog requires: failure is of a reachable object.

Thus:

> **The third member is possibility. The writing can be understood. Therefore it can be misread. The catalog does not abolish knowledge. It locates the operations by which knowledge of the writing is missed.**

---

# 67.13 Mode I — Poor Perception

Poor perception is the first mode because nothing later can be sound if the writing is not first received as what is there.

Perception, in this argument, is the intake of the presented thing: the words as written, the fact that a statement has been made, the visible relations on the page or in the hearing, the memory of what has already been shown. It is the operation Chapters 4–6 already required as the beginning of knowledge. Applied to Scripture, it is the beginning of knowing the scriptures.

Poor perception is not illiteracy as such. A man may be able to sound the words and still not see what they present. Poor perception is not the absence of a copy. The disciples in Mark 8 had been present for the breakings of bread. They had eyes. They had ears. The rebuke is that those organs were not in use toward what had been done and said. Poor perception is refused intake.

Poor perception may be dullness: the words pass and leave no mark. It may be selective: the eye catches the useful fragment and does not register the neighbour that governs it. It may be hardened: the heart has already decided what must not be seen. Mark 8 joins perception, understanding, hardness, seeing, hearing, and memory in one rebuke. The join is important. Hardness is named as a cause of not seeing. Not seeing is still the first failed operation.

The mode is already a misreading when the writing is not seen as the writing it is. A people may handle a volume and not perceive that a command was given, that a promise was made, that a speaker was Satan, that a question was asked, or that a resurrection was stated in “I am the God of Abraham.” The later modes will fail because the first intake failed.

Thus:

> **Poor perception is refused or neglected intake of what the writing presents. It is the first mode. Later grasp, inference, context, and handling cannot repair what was never seen.**

---

# 67.14 Biblical Record: Mark 8:17–18

Mark 8:14–21 records a crossing after the feedings. The disciples had forgotten to take bread. Jesus charged them: “Take heed, beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, and of the leaven of Herod.” They reasoned among themselves, saying, “It is because we have no bread.” He, knowing it, said:

> “Why reason ye, because ye have no bread? perceive ye not yet, neither understand? have ye your heart yet hardened? Having eyes, see ye not? and having ears, hear ye not? and do ye not remember?”

He then recalled the five thousand and the four thousand, the baskets taken up, and asked again, “How is it that ye do not understand?”

**Context.** The speaker is Jesus. The audience is disciples who have just seen two feedings. The occasion is a warning about leaven — teaching and corruption, as Matthew 16:12 will state when the same incident is understood. The surrounding argument is not a lesson about bakery. It is a lesson about a kind of influence, given to men who have already been shown that bread is not the limiting fact.

**What is explicit.** He names a failure to perceive, a failure to understand, a hardened heart, unused eyes, unused ears, and unused memory. He treats those as willful in the sense that the organs and the prior evidence were present. He treats their reasoning about bread as the wrong operation toward His sentence.

**What the passage warrants for this mode.** Perception is an operation that can be refused while eyes and ears remain. Memory of what the same speaker has already shown belongs to perception of His present sentence. A warning can be in the ear and not in the intake. The first mode is live among possessors, not only among outsiders.

**What the passage does not warrant here.** That disciples are *apeiros* as a finished diagnosis. That remaining labour-files have been written. That every later failure is hardness. Hardness is named in this scene. It is not the whole catalog.

Thus:

> **Mark 8:17–18 warrants poor perception as a named operation: eyes and ears present, intake refused, memory unused, a sentence in the ear and not received as what it is.**

---

# 67.15 Biblical Record: Matthew 13:13–15 and Isaiah 6:9–10

Matthew 13:13–15 gives Jesus’ reason for speaking to the multitude in parables:

> “Therefore speak I to them in parables: because they seeing see not; and hearing they hear not, neither do they understand.”

He then cites Isaiah 6:9–10: hearing but not understanding, seeing but not perceiving, a heart waxed gross, ears dull of hearing, eyes closed, lest they be converted and He heal them.

**Context.** The speaker is Jesus, after the parable of the sower, answering why He speaks as He does. The cited writing is Isaiah’s commission, where the prophet is sent to a people who will hear and not understand. The audience of Matthew 13 includes a multitude and, separately, disciples who ask and receive explanation. The same chapter records, “Who hath ears to hear, let him hear,” and the explanation that the wicked one catches away what was sown in the heart when a man “understandeth it not” (Matthew 13:19).

**What is explicit.** Seeing without seeing and hearing without hearing are named. Understanding is named as what does not occur. The heart, ears, and eyes are named as the organs of the failure. Conversion and healing are named as what the closed organs refuse.

**What the passage warrants for this mode.** Poor perception is not a modern psychological label laid on the text. It is the text’s own pairing of organs with refused intake. The pairing is moral and volitional in Isaiah’s wording: eyes closed, ears dull, heart gross. The reconstructible Introduction proposition that the reasons the Bible is not understood are willful operations finds correspondence here: the organs are not missing; they are unused toward the communication.

**What the passage does not warrant here.** That parables make the writing a book of remaining mysteries. Matthew 13 also records explanation given to those who ask. That dullness of hearing has been examined as Hebrews 5’s dedicated diagnosis. Neighbourhood is not arrival. That every later reader who finds a sentence hard has already closed his eyes in Isaiah’s sense. Hardness of a passage and closing of eyes are two.

Thus:

> **Matthew 13:13–15 and Isaiah 6:9–10 warrant poor perception as seeing without seeing and hearing without hearing — organs present, intake refused, understanding therefore not reached.**

---

# 67.16 Biblical Record: John 8:43

John 8:43: “Why do ye not understand my speech? even because ye cannot hear my word.”

**Context.** The speaker is Jesus, in dispute with hearers who claim Abraham as father and who have not believed. The surrounding argument includes “If ye continue in my word, then are ye my disciples indeed; and ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free” (John 8:31–32), and the later charge that they are of their father the devil, a liar and the father of it (John 8:44). Speech and word are distinguished in the verse itself: λαλιά (*lalia*) as the uttered speech; λόγος (*logos*) as the word they cannot hear.

**What is explicit.** Failure to understand speech is traced to inability to hear the word. The inability is not presented as a missing lexicon. It is presented as a moral-spiritual refusal inside a dispute about truth, freedom, and fatherhood.

**What the passage warrants for this mode.** Understanding of uttered speech depends on hearing the word that the speech carries. A man may have the sounds and not have the hearing. Poor perception, at this depth, is not only unused eyes. It is unused hearing of the word. John 8:32 also warrants the counterpart already used as third member: truth known frees. The writing’s communication is not a prison of obscurity.

**What the passage does not warrant here.** That every grammatical difficulty is John 8:43. That the First Principles have been taught because “truth makes free” has been cited. That institutional aridity has been examined. The verse is mode-evidence: speech not understood because the word is not heard.

Thus:

> **John 8:43 warrants the first mode at the hearing of the word: speech can be in the air and the word not heard; understanding then fails because intake of the word failed.**

---

# 67.17 Mode II — Deficient Understanding

Deficient understanding is the second mode because a writing may be perceived as words and still not grasped as sense.

Understanding, in this argument, is the grasp of what the perceived writing communicates: the meaning of the words in their relations, the force of the statement, the thing asserted, commanded, promised, or asked. It is not a second inspiration. It is not authority over the text. Chapter 66 already established that understanding is reception, not rule. The present file examines the failure of that reception.

Deficient understanding is the operation Matthew 22:29 names as not knowing the scriptures. Possession is not the knowledge. The Sadducees handle Moses. They do not know what Moses communicates concerning the living God and therefore concerning the dead. Deficient understanding is also the operation Acts 8 names when a man reads Isaiah aloud and answers that he cannot understand except some man should guide him. The reading is real. The grasp is not yet real.

Deficient understanding may follow poor perception. It may also follow perception of words without comparison, without the rest of the subject, or without the speaker’s own later light on the same matter. Luke 24 records hearers who had the prophets and were slow of heart to believe what the prophets had spoken. The writings stood. The grasp had not occurred. He then, beginning at Moses and all the prophets, expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning Himself. Exposition here is sense given toward writings that already communicated. It is not a second Graphē.

The reconstructible Introduction proposition that the Bible is self-interpreting in the sense that its so-called mysteries are explained by the writings themselves, and that passages generally have one simple meaning, belongs here as a claim to be tested, not as a charm. If the writings communicate, understanding is grasp of that communication, not invention of a second meaning. If a passage has a double meaning, the writings themselves make that fact clear. Deficient understanding includes treating a clear communication as if it had not been given, and treating a figurative communication as if no literal truth were intended.

Thus:

> **Deficient understanding is failure to grasp the sense of a writing that communicates. Words may be in hand. Knowledge of the scriptures is not thereby in hand.**

---

# 67.18 Biblical Record: Matthew 22:29 — Ye Do Err, Not Knowing the Scriptures

Matthew 22:23–33 records Sadducees, who say there is no resurrection, putting a case of seven brothers and one wife, and asking whose wife she shall be in the resurrection. Jesus answered:

> “Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of God.”

He then states that in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, and, as touching the resurrection of the dead, appeals to what was spoken by God: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” God is not the God of the dead, but of the living. Mark 12:24, 27 records the same rebuke and the same appeal, and adds, “ye therefore do greatly err.”

**Context.** The speaker is Jesus. The audience is a party that denies resurrection and uses Moses as a puzzle against it. The occasion is a public dispute. The cited writing is Exodus 3:6, in the bush, where God identifies Himself by the patriarchs. The surrounding argument is not a licence to invent a resurrection-doctrine from a mood. It is a reasoning from what is written: the identification “I am” of patriarchs who had died as to the body is unintelligible if they have perished as persons.

**What is explicit.** Error is named. The cause named is not knowing the scriptures, and not knowing the power of God. The scriptures they do not know are scriptures they handle. The correction is itself a use of what is written.

**What the passage warrants for this mode.** Deficient understanding is compatible with handling Moses. Possession of the writings is not knowledge of the writings. Error is the later act. The writings and the power of God are not the error. Chapter 66 already used this scene as exhibition that possessors can err. The present file uses it as the second mode’s primary warrant: the operation named is not-knowing, and the not-knowing is of scriptures already in hand.

**What the passage does not warrant here.** That every eschatological disagreement is this scene. That tradition as a system has been examined because Sadducees are a party. Party is the speaker. Mode is the not-knowing.

Thus:

> **Matthew 22:29 warrants deficient understanding as not knowing the scriptures while handling them. Error is named. The writings remain the measure and the correction.**

---

# 67.19 Biblical Record: Acts 8:30–35

Acts 8:27–35 records a man of Ethiopia, a eunuch of great authority, sitting in his chariot and reading Esaias the prophet. The Spirit said to Philip, Go near. Philip ran thither and heard him read, and said:

> “Understandest thou what thou readest?”

The eunuch said:

> “How can I, except some man should guide me?”

He had been reading Isaiah 53:7–8. He asked of whom the prophet spoke, of himself or of some other man. Philip opened his mouth, and began at the same scripture, and preached unto him Jesus.

**Context.** The reader is a man already possessing and reading the writing. The guide is not a second source of revelation beside the writing. He begins at the same scripture. The occasion is a reading of a prophetic passage whose subject the reader has not yet identified. The surrounding narrative includes the Spirit’s sending and, after the sense is given, baptism. Those later acts do not convert the scene into the First Principles or into a baptism-file. They locate the reading as a real reading that needed grasp.

**What is explicit.** Reading and understanding are distinguished. Guidance is requested as help toward the reading, not as replacement of the reading. The same scripture is the starting-point of the explanation. The question “of whom” is a question about the writing’s subject.

**What the passage warrants for this mode.** Deficient understanding can be honest. The eunuch is not named as a wrestler. He is named as a reader who does not yet grasp. The distinction between difficulty and wresting, already required, has a scene. Guidance that begins at the same scripture is interpretation in Chapter 66’s defined sense: accountable sense-giving toward a writing that remains the object. The scene also warrants the third member again: understanding can be given. The catalog of failure includes a failure that is not yet a crime, and that can be remedied by the writing’s own communication opened.

**What the passage does not warrant here.** That an office of guides is a second Graphē. That Movement X’s labour-files have been written because a guide appears. That every reader who asks for help is thereby *nēpios* as a finished diagnosis.

Thus:

> **Acts 8:30–35 warrants deficient understanding as reading without grasp, and warrants help as sense given from the same writing, not as a second writing.**
