# 67.20 Biblical Record: Luke 24:25–27, 44–45

Luke 24:25–27 records the risen Christ saying to the two on the way:

> “O fools, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken: Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and to enter into his glory?”

And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, He expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning Himself.

Luke 24:44–45 records, to the eleven and them that were with them:

> “These are the words which I spake unto you, while I was yet with you, that all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me.”

Then opened He their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures.

**Context.** The writings already stood. Moses, the prophets, and the psalms are named as the already-written field. The hearers are disciples who have the writings and the prior spoken words, and who are slow to believe what those writings had spoken. The operation He performs is exposition in the writings, and opening of understanding toward those writings.

**What is explicit.** Slowness of heart is named. Belief of all that the prophets have spoken is what was lacking. Exposition is in all the scriptures. Understanding is opened so that the scriptures might be understood. The writings are the object before and after the opening.

**What the passage warrants for this mode.** Deficient understanding may be slowness toward writings that already communicate the very thing not grasped. The deficiency is not the writings’ emptiness. The remedy is not a replacement writing. The remedy is understanding opened toward the same corpus. Chapter 66 already used this scene as two objects: writings that stand, understanding that may be opened. The present file uses it as mode-evidence: the failed operation is slowness to grasp what the prophets have spoken.

**What the passage does not warrant here.** That opening of understanding has been examined as a dedicated labour-stage. That “all the scriptures” has been rewritten as a second “all Scripture” file. Chapter 31 remains the “all” file. That every later exposition is thereby Christ. The scene warrants the mode and the possibility of grasp. It does not baptize later mouths.

Thus:

> **Luke 24 warrants deficient understanding as slowness toward writings that already speak, and warrants understanding as grasp of those same writings, not as their replacement.**

---

# 67.21 Mode III — Faulty Inference

Faulty inference is the third mode because a writing may be perceived and even partly understood, and a conclusion may still be drawn that the writing does not warrant.

Inference, in this argument, is the movement from premises to a conclusion. Chapters 5–6 already distinguished valid from invalid inference, deduction, induction, analogy, and the common failures: equivocation, non sequitur, false dichotomy, begging the question. Applied to Scripture, faulty inference is that movement performed so that a conclusion is attached to a text as if the text had given it, when the text has not given it.

Faulty inference is not the existence of inference. The writings themselves infer. Christ infers from “I am the God of Abraham” to the living. The Bereans search whether those things were so — a whether that is itself an inferential test. Faulty inference is the invalid step.

The typical forms in this file are few and sufficient.

**Wrong object.** A sentence about one thing is taken as a sentence about another. “Leaven” is taken as “bread.” “This temple” is taken as Herod’s stones when the speaker speaks of His body.

**Invalid step.** A genuine sentence is granted, and a command or doctrine is attached that does not follow. Psalm 91:11–12 is genuine. “Cast thyself down” does not follow as a duty.

**Over-extension.** A true particular is made a universal the text does not state, or a true universal is denied by a particular the text does not isolate as a cancellation.

**Under-extension.** A statement that governs a subject is restricted to a fragment that leaves the subject ungoverned.

**Speaker-confusion as inference.** A recorded lie is treated as a premise of truth because it is in the writing. Chapter 56 already required speaker-distinction as inspiration’s guarantee: inspiration records what was said; it does not baptize every speaker. Using Satan’s sentence as a divine command is a faulty inference from presence in the record to divine endorsement.

Thus:

> **Faulty inference is an invalid step from a writing, or from a fragment of a writing, to a conclusion the communication does not warrant. The text used may be genuine. The step is still a misreading.**

# 67.22 Biblical Record: Matthew 16:6–12

Matthew 16:5–12 records the same crossing-warning as Mark 8, with the conclusion stated. Jesus said, “Take heed and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and of the Sadducees.” They reasoned among themselves, saying, “It is because we have taken no bread.” He rebukes their little faith and their failure to remember the five thousand and the four thousand, and asks how they do not understand that He spake not of bread. Then they understood how that He bade them not beware of the leaven of bread, but of the doctrine of the Pharisees and of the Sadducees.

**Context.** The speaker’s sentence is a warning about teaching. The disciples’ inference is about provisions. The surrounding argument includes prior miracles that already answered the provision-worry. The correction is not a new writing. It is the same sentence understood.

**What is explicit.** They reasoned. The reasoning is named as the wrong conclusion. Understanding later consists in grasping that the warning was about doctrine, not bread.

**What the passage warrants for this mode.** A genuine sentence can be in the ear, and the inference drawn from it can be false. “They reasoned among themselves” is not already sound judgment. Chapter 6 already required that reasoning be examined as reasoning. The present scene is that requirement applied to a sentence of Christ. Faulty inference here is not wresting as a completed corruption. It is a miss of the referent. The miss is still a misreading of the sentence they heard.

**What the passage does not warrant here.** That every figurative word has been catalogued. That doctrine as a system-file has been written because “doctrine of the Pharisees” appears. The word here is teaching as leaven, used as the correct referent. The system-file remains later.

Thus:

> **Matthew 16:6–12 warrants faulty inference as reasoning from a genuine sentence to the wrong object. Understanding is the sentence grasped. The false step is the misreading.**

# 67.23 Biblical Record: John 2:19–22

John 2:19–22 records Jesus answering the Jews who demanded a sign: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” Then said the Jews, “Forty and six years was this temple in building, and wilt thou rear it up in three days?” But He spake of the temple of His body. When therefore He was risen from the dead, His disciples remembered that He had said this unto them; and they believed the scripture, and the word which Jesus had said.

**Context.** The speaker is Jesus, in the temple, after the cleansing. The audience takes “temple” as the building in which they stand. The narrator states the intended referent: His body. The later remembrance of disciples joins “the scripture” and “the word which Jesus had said.”

**What is explicit.** A genuine sentence is heard. A conclusion about Herod’s stones is drawn. That conclusion is not what He spake. The body is what He spake. Later belief includes both scripture and His word, remembered after the resurrection.

**What the passage warrants for this mode.** Faulty inference may be a wrong referent attached to a true sentence. The sentence is not emptied by being misunderstood. The disciples’ later remembrance is not a licence to treat all later readings as equally delayed. It is evidence that a sentence can stand, be misread as to referent, and later be grasped as what it was.

**What the passage does not warrant here.** That every temple-saying in Scripture is this saying. That figurative language has no literal truth: the literal truth here is His body raised. The figure is the word “temple” used of that body. The reconstructible Introduction rule — when language is figurative, get the literal truth conveyed — has a scene.

Thus:

> **John 2:19–22 warrants faulty inference as a wrong referent attached to a genuine sentence, and warrants the sentence’s standing through the miss. The literal truth intended is not the hearers’ building-inference.**

# 67.24 Biblical Record: Matthew 4:5–7 — A True Writing Used for a False Step

Matthew 4:5–7 records the devil taking Jesus into the holy city, setting Him on a pinnacle of the temple, and saying:

> “If thou be the Son of God, cast thyself down: for it is written, He shall give his angels charge concerning thee: and in their hands they shall bear thee up, lest at any time thou dash thy foot against a stone.”

Jesus said unto him, “It is written again, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.”

The cited writing is Psalm 91:11–12. The answering writing is Deuteronomy 6:16.

**Context.** The speaker of the citation is the tempter. The audience is the Son. The occasion is temptation after the forty days. The cited psalm promises angelic charge in the ways of trust, not a command to manufacture a fall in order to force a proof. The answering sentence forbids tempting the Lord. Luke 4:9–12 records the same exchange.

**What is explicit.** “It is written” can be in a later mouth that is not thereby the writing. A genuine psalm is cited. A command to cast Himself down is attached. The Son answers by another writing, not by denying that the psalm is written.

**What the passage warrants for this mode.** Faulty inference may be performed with a true citation. The invalid step is the movement from angelic charge to a duty to leap. Context failure is already neighbouring: the psalm is not a licence to tempt God. Improper handling is already neighbouring: the writing is used to urge what the writings forbid. The scene is placed under inference because the live operation exhibited is the false step from a cited sentence to a commanded act. The other modes are present as materials. The inference is the step that must be refused.

The scene also warrants the already-earned distinction of quotation from the writing. Chapter 66 established that quotation is not the Graphē. The present file uses that conclusion as mode-evidence: the tempter quotes and misreads. Citation is not correctness.

**What the passage does not warrant here.** That every later citation is satanic. That Psalm 91 has been emptied of promise. The promise stands. The step fails. That spiritual warfare has been written as a system. The mode is the false step.

Thus:

> **Matthew 4:5–7 warrants faulty inference from a genuine writing to an unwarranted act. “It is written” in a later mouth is not, by itself, a true use. Another writing judges the step.**

# 67.25 Mode IV — Context Failure

Context failure is the fourth mode because a sentence of a communicating writing has a location, and isolation treats it as if it had none.

**Context**, in this argument, is the writing’s own placement of a statement among the things that govern its sense: the speaker, the audience, the occasion, the surrounding argument, the wording and grammar, the literary form, the historical setting where the writing itself requires it, and the other scriptures that bear upon the same subject. The biblical-context protocol of the governing methodology is this list. It is not a later academic fashion imposed on a book that has no neighbours.

Context failure is the operation of refusing that placement. The typical form is the isolated sentence: a clause is lifted, used, and made to govern a subject its neighbours do not permit it to govern, or made to mean what its speaker does not say. Other forms include ignoring who is speaking, ignoring to whom it is spoken, ignoring the occasion, ignoring the argument in which the sentence is a step, and ignoring the rest of the corpus on the same matter.

Context failure is already a misreading when the isolated sentence is true as a sentence and false as used. Psalm 91:11–12 is true in the psalm. Isolated as a command to leap, it is a failed use. “Destroy this temple” is true as spoken of His body. Isolated as a claim about Herod’s stones, it is a failed use. “I am the God of Abraham” is true in Exodus 3. Isolated from the force of “I am” toward the patriarchs, it is a sentence the Sadducees can possess without knowing.

The reconstructible Introduction rule that all scriptures on a subject must be harmonized, and that a doctrine out of harmony with any one written statement is false, belongs here as a tested proposition about context in the wide sense: the corpus is a neighbour of the sentence. The law of two or three witnesses, stated in Deuteronomy 19:15 and used of testimony in Matthew 18:16 and 2 Corinthians 13:1, will be tested below as a related discipline: a later doctrine is not established by one isolated usefulness. Those propositions are not yet the labour-file of rightly dividing. They are the reason isolation is a mode of misreading.

Thus:

> **Context failure is refusal of the writing’s own placement of a sentence. Isolation is the typical form. A true clause, cut from its neighbours, becomes a false use.**

---

# 67.26 Biblical Record: Genesis 3:1–5 — The First Distortion of What Was Said

Genesis 2:16–17 records the command: of every tree of the garden the man may freely eat; of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, he shall not eat; in the day he eats, he shall surely die. Genesis 3:1–5 records the serpent’s questions and claims:

> “Yea, hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden?”

The woman answers with a narrowed permission, an added “neither shall ye touch it,” and a softened “lest ye die.” The serpent answers, “Ye shall not surely die,” and attaches a purpose: God knows that in the day ye eat, your eyes shall be opened, and ye shall be as gods, knowing good and evil.

**Context.** The speaker of the command is God. The speaker of the question and the denial is the serpent. The audience is the woman, with the man. The occasion is the first recorded distortion of a given word. The surrounding argument of the book is not a parable of reading-theory. It is a historical account of a command, a distortion, and a fall. The present file uses the scene as the record’s first exhibition of a later mouth handling a given word by questioning, adding, softening, and reversing.

**What is explicit.** The command was given with a permission, a prohibition, and a penalty. The later handling questions whether God has said, alters the scope, adds a clause, weakens the penalty, then denies the penalty and assigns a rival motive to God.

**What the passage warrants for this mode.** Context failure begins when the given wording is no longer the measure of the later sentence about it. “Hath God said” is already a move to detach the later discussion from the given wording. Addition and subtraction are already mishandling of neighbours: “every tree” and “surely die” were neighbours of the prohibition. The scene also warrants improper handling and faulty inference as materials: the denial is a false conclusion about the command; the handling is a use of the field of God’s word to evacuate God’s word. It is placed under context because the first operation exhibited is the displacement of the given wording by a later version of the wording.

**What the passage does not warrant here.** That every later question about a text is the serpent’s question. Isaiah 1:18 remains an invitation to reason. Testing a sermon by the writings remains noble. The serpent’s question is not a search whether those things were so. It is a loosening of whether God has said what God has said. That later systems of temptation have been examined. The mode is the distortion of a given word.

Thus:

> **Genesis 3:1–5 warrants context failure as the first distortion of a given word: questioning the wording, adding, softening, reversing. The given command remains the measure of the later version.**

---

# 67.27 The Isolated Sentence and the Missing Neighbours

Isolation is the ordinary form of context failure in later use.

A sentence is isolated when it is made to do work its neighbours forbid, or to refrain from work its neighbours require. The work may be a doctrine, a permission, a threat, a promise, or a command. The isolation may be of a clause, a verse, a word, or a scene. The form does not matter. The missing neighbours do.

Neighbours include the immediate sentences. Psalm 91’s “in all thy ways” and the psalm’s character as trust, not as a dare, are neighbours of the angelic-charge sentences. Neighbours include the speaker. “Ye shall not surely die” is a neighbour of the command only as a contrary later mouth, not as a second divine sentence. Neighbours include the rest of the subject. A sentence about faith that is cut from the sentences about obedience, or a sentence about grace that is cut from the sentences about sin, is already a context failure even when each isolated clause is true as a clause.

The reconstructible Introduction proposition that the Bible is not a book of systematic discourses on any one subject, but that one must collect, from here and there, all God’s information through various writers in order to know the whole truth, belongs here as a tested claim about neighbours in the wide sense. If the proposition is sound, isolation of one writer’s sentence from the rest of the subject is a mode of missing the whole truth the writings give. The present file does not convert that proposition into a finished topical method. It uses it as warrant against isolation: a communicating corpus is not used as a communicating corpus when one useful clause is made to silence the rest.

Isolation often presents itself as reverence: “the verse says.” The verse may say. The use may still be a miss of what the writing says. “The verse says” is perception of a clause. Context is perception of the writing.

Thus:

> **Isolation is context failure in ordinary form. A true clause without its neighbours is already a false use when the neighbours govern the clause’s force.**

---

# 67.28 Speaker, Audience, Occasion, and Scope

Four particular neighbours must be named because their absence is a common form of the fourth mode.

**Speaker.** Inspiration records God, Christ, prophets, apostles, holy men, and also Satan, demons, and men speaking lies or errors. Chapter 56 already established that inspiration guarantees the accuracy of the record of what was said, not the truth of every recorded claim. To treat a recorded lie as a divine premise is context failure at the speaker. To treat a recorded human question as a revealed assertion is the same failure in a milder form.

**Audience.** A command given to a particular man, people, or office is not, by being written, already a command of the same force to every later reader without the writing’s own extension. Scope is part of sense. The present file does not write the later labour of dividing times and classes as a finished file. It names the failure: a sentence spoken to one audience, used as if audience were nothing, is already a miss of the writing’s placement.

**Occasion.** A sentence answering a trap, a grief, a request, or a controversy has that occasion as a neighbour. Matthew 22:29 is an answer to a resurrection-denying puzzle. To use “ye do err” as a charm against every opponent, without the scriptures and the power of God as the named cause, is already to isolate the rebuke from its occasion.

**Scope.** Universal statements and particular statements are not interchangeable. “All Scripture” is a scope already controlled in Chapter 31. A particular narrative is a particular narrative. Context failure includes making the particular do the work of the universal, and making the universal collapse into an anecdote.

The reconstructible Introduction rule that truth must be divided with regard for times, classes, and subjects is named here only as coherence with scope. The dedicated file of rightly dividing remains later. The present point is already full: ignoring speaker, audience, occasion, or scope is already a misreading.

Thus:

> **Speaker, audience, occasion, and scope are neighbours. Treating them as nothing is context failure. Naming them is not yet the labour-file of rightly dividing.**

---

# 67.29 Mode V — Improper Handling

Improper handling is the fifth mode because a writing may be perceived, partly understood, inferred from, and even placed among some neighbours, and still be used so as to evacuate what it communicates.

**Handling**, in this argument, is the use of the writing as writing: citing it, teaching it, applying it, arguing from it, translating its force into a later claim or a later life. Chapter 66 already established that such use is a later act. The present file examines the use that fails as use.

Improper handling includes, as the writings name it:

- **Wresting** — twisting the writing’s force so that the handler is destroyed by the handling (2 Peter 3:16).
- **Corrupting** — treating the word as merchandise or as material to be diluted (2 Corinthians 2:17).
- **Deceitful handling** — using the word as a cover for a hidden claim (2 Corinthians 4:2).
- **Making the word of none effect** — occupying the field of the word while laying the word aside (Mark 7:13).
- **Changing a communicated sense into a second sense the writing does not give** — spiritualizing a historical statement into a denial of the history, or literalizing a figure so as to miss the literal truth the figure conveys.
- **Using the writing to further a later interest** — the writing as instrument of the handler rather than as measure of the handler.

Improper handling is the completed form toward which the other modes tend. Poor perception supplies unused words. Deficient understanding supplies unused sense. Faulty inference supplies a false step. Context failure supplies an isolated clause. Improper handling is those materials used as if they were the writing’s force.

The reconstructible Introduction rule — take the Bible literally wherein it is at all possible; if symbolic, figurative, or typical language is used, then look for the literal truth it intends to convey; never change the literal meaning to a spiritual, mystical, symbolic, or figurative meaning unless the writing itself does so — belongs here as a tested discipline of handling. The rule is not a denial that figures exist. The writings contain parables, symbols, types, and figures. The rule is a refusal to treat “the writing says this” as “the writing means the opposite,” and a refusal to treat a figure as a licence to evacuate history. Novel interpretations supported by personal opinion alone are, in those same materials, to be laid aside. That refusal is handling-discipline, not a system-file.

Thus:

> **Improper handling is the writing used against its own communication — twisted, diluted, made a cover, laid aside while occupied, or exchanged for a second meaning the text does not give. The other modes are often its materials.**

---

# 67.30 Biblical Record: 2 Peter 3:16 — Wresting the Scriptures

2 Peter 3:15–16 records that Paul, according to the wisdom given unto him, has written, “as also in all his epistles, speaking in them of these things; in which are some things hard to be understood, which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest, as they do also the other scriptures, unto their own destruction.”

**Context.** The speaker is Peter. The audience is believers who have a pure mind and who are to be mindful of the words spoken before by the holy prophets and of the commandment of the apostles (2 Peter 3:1–2). The occasion includes scoffers and the promise of the Lord’s coming. The surrounding argument treats Paul’s writings as already among “the other scriptures.” Chapter 52 already used that recognition. The present file uses the handling named.

The verb is στρεβλόω (*strebloō*, G4761): to twist, wrench, torture; in this use, to wrest writings. The handlers are ἀμαθεῖς and ἀστήρικτοι — unlearned and unstable. The result is their own destruction. The objects include things hard to be understood, and also the other scriptures.

**What is explicit.** Hardness is named. Wresting is named. The wresting is of writings that already stand, including writings already classed with the other scriptures. The destruction is the handlers’. The writings are not said to be destroyed.

**What the passage warrants for this mode.** Improper handling is a real operation toward a standing corpus. Hardness of some things is not unintelligibility of the corpus, and it is not a licence to twist. Unlearned and unstable name the handlers’ condition. They do not name a finished *apeiros*-file. They name that wresting is not the act of a writing that failed, but of handlers who twist. Chapter 66 already used the scene as two objects. The present file uses it as the fifth mode’s primary warrant: wresting is the named handling.

**What the passage does not warrant here.** That every hard passage has been listed. That unskillfulness has been examined as Hebrews 5’s dedicated object. That accepted heresies have been catalogued because destruction is named. Destruction is the result named. The heresy-file remains later.

Thus:

> **2 Peter 3:16 warrants improper handling as wresting of writings that stand, including hard things and the other scriptures, unto the handlers’ destruction. Hardness is not the wresting. The writings remain the object.**

---

# 67.31 Biblical Record: 2 Corinthians 2:17 and 4:2

2 Corinthians 2:17: “For we are not as many, which corrupt the word of God: but as of sincerity, but as of God, in the sight of God speak we in Christ.”

2 Corinthians 4:2: “But have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man’s conscience in the sight of God.”

2 Corinthians 4:3–4 continues that if the gospel be hid, it is hid to them that are lost, in whom the god of this world hath blinded the minds of them which believe not.

**Context.** The speaker is Paul, defending a ministry of the new covenant against those who peddle or dilute the word, and against a hidden, crafty use of the word. The verb in 2:17 is καπηλεύω (*kapēleuō*, G2585): to peddle, to retail as a huckster, to corrupt by mixing. The handling in 4:2 is δόλος (*dolos*): deceit. The contrast is sincerity, manifestation of the truth, speech as of God in the sight of God.

**What is explicit.** The word of God can be corrupted by many. The word of God can be handled deceitfully. A contrary ministry refuses both. Blindness of minds is named as a further operation upon those who believe not.

**What the passage warrants for this mode.** Improper handling includes commercial or diluting use and deceitful use. The word remains the word while being so handled. Sincerity is named as the contrary manner of speech, not as a determinant of truth — Chapters 1–3 already forbade sincerity to baptize a claim. Here sincerity is the refused mixture: the word not cut with a later interest. Blindness of minds neighbours poor perception without converting this scene into Isaiah 6 rewritten.

**What the passage does not warrant here.** That every paid teacher is thereby a corrupter. The verb names a kind of use, not a wage. That Movement X has been written because manifestation of the truth appears. Manifestation is the contrary of deceitful handling.

Thus:

> **2 Corinthians 2:17 and 4:2 warrant improper handling as corrupting and as deceitful use of the word of God. The word remains the measure of the use. Sincerity here is refused mixture, not a baptism of error.**

---

# 67.32 Biblical Record: Mark 7 and Matthew 15 as Handling That Evacuates

Mark 7:6–13 and Matthew 15:3–9 record Jesus answering a tradition-charge about unwashed hands by a counter-charge: well hath Isaiah prophesied, “This people honoureth me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. Howbeit in vain do they worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.” They lay aside the commandment of God and hold the tradition of men. Moses said, Honour thy father and thy mother. The later device of Corban is used so that a man does no more for father or mother. “Making the word of God of none effect through your tradition.”

**Context.** The speaker is Jesus. The audience is Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem, and then the multitude. The occasion is a dispute about tradition as a measure of defilement. The cited writings are Isaiah 29:13 and the command to honour father and mother. Chapter 66 already used the scene as two objects: the word of God and the tradition of men. The present file uses the handling: the word is occupied as a field and laid aside as a force.

**What is explicit.** Lip-honour can accompany a far heart. Commandments of men can be taught as doctrines. The commandment of God can be laid aside. The word of God can be made of none effect through a later tradition. A particular command is named as the evacuated thing.

**What the passage warrants for this mode.** Improper handling includes a use that leaves the writing’s words in the field and removes their force. The later claim is not examined here as a system of tradition. It is examined as a handling: the word used so as to be of none effect. Context failure is neighbouring: the command to honour parents is a neighbour the later device refuses. The fifth mode is the completed evacuation.

**What the passage does not warrant here.** That Chapter 68 has been written. Tradition as a system remains later. That Chapter 69 has been written. Displacement as a finished file remains later. The scene is mode-evidence: handling that evacuates.

Thus:

> **Mark 7 and Matthew 15 warrant improper handling as making the word of God of none effect while occupying the field of the word. The word remains the measure. The later system-file remains later.**

---

# 67.33 Literal Sense, Figurative Language, and the Invented Second Meaning

A live form of improper handling, neighbouring context failure and faulty inference, is the exchange of a communicated sense for a second sense the writing does not give.

Two contrary abuses must be refused together.

**Spiritualizing against the communication.** A historical statement, a command, a promise, or a prophecy is treated as if the writing meant something else, usually something that leaves the stated thing unasserted. The reconstructible Introduction rule refuses this exchange except where the writing itself uses symbolic, figurative, or typical language. The rule is sound as handling-discipline if the writing is a communicating writing and not a book that says one thing and means another. The same materials state that generally the passages have one simple meaning, and that in the few which have a double meaning the fact is clear from the verses or from parallel passages. That claim is tested as coherence with a communicating corpus, not as a charm that no figure exists.

**Literalizing a figure so as to miss the literal truth the figure conveys.** Parables, symbols, types, and figures are in the writings. “Leaven” in Matthew 16 is a figure whose literal truth is doctrine. “Temple” in John 2:19 is a figure whose literal truth is His body. To insist on Herod’s stones is not fidelity to the letter. It is a miss of the communication. The Introduction rule’s second clause is this refusal: when the language cannot be taken literally, get the literal truth conveyed by the figurative language.

The two abuses share one operation: the handler, not the writing, becomes the giver of the sense. Novel interpretation supported by personal opinion alone is that operation named as a method. The present file refuses the method as improper handling. It does not write a complete hermeneutical manual. Movement X remains that labour.

A related form is the claim that the Bible is a book of remaining mysteries, so that a later decoder is required before any sense can be had. The reconstructible Introduction proposition that the Bible explains its so-called mysteries and is so self-interpreting that no mystery remains as an unintelligible residue must be tested, not shouted. What it warrants here is limited and full: the writing is not a sealed charm; later decoding is not a second Graphē; hardness of some things (2 Peter 3:16) is not a remaining unintelligible residue that baptizes every later invention. What it does not warrant here is that every reader already understands every sentence, or that Hebrews 5’s milk and meat have been examined.

Thus:

> **Improper handling includes exchanging the communicated sense for a second sense the writing does not give — whether by spiritualizing away what is said, or by missing the literal truth a figure conveys. Opinion is not the court. The writing is the court.**

---

# 67.34 Who Is Speaking: Inspiration Records Without Baptizing Every Speaker

Speaker-distinction, already a guarantee of inspiration in Chapter 56, is now a rule against a live mishandling.

The writings record the language of God, of Christ, of the Spirit, of angels, of prophets, of apostles, and also of Satan, of demons, and of men. Inspiration guarantees that what is recorded as said was said as recorded. It does not place all that is said on the same level of truth required for obedience. A recorded lie remains a lie. A recorded fallacy remains a fallacy. A recorded crime remains a crime. The record of those things is true as record. The things recorded are not thereby true as doctrine.

Misreading at this point is a faulty inference from presence in the Graphē to divine endorsement, and it is an improper handling of the record as if every sentence were a premise of the same kind. Genesis 3:4 is in the writing. “Ye shall not surely die” is not therefore a promise of God. Matthew 4:6 is in the writing. The tempter’s use of Psalm 91 is not therefore a command of God. Job’s friends speak many sentences. The end of the book judges their counsel. The Sadducees’ puzzle is in the writing. The puzzle is not the doctrine of the resurrection.

The rule is not cynicism about the record. It is fidelity to the record. A writing that accurately records a lie has told the truth about the lie. A reader who obeys the lie because it is printed has not become more biblical. He has misread the record’s speaker.

Thus:

> **Speaker-distinction is a handling-rule. Presence in the writing is not endorsement of every speaker. The record of a lie is true as record. The lie is not truth.**

---

# 67.35 Comparing Scripture with Scripture: The Two-or-Three Witness Rule

A further handling-discipline belongs to the fifth mode as the refusal of its ordinary material: the single useful clause.

Deuteronomy 19:15 requires that a matter be established at the mouth of two or three witnesses. Matthew 18:16 uses the same requirement of testimony. 2 Corinthians 13:1 uses it of a word established. The reconstructible Introduction proposition that this states a law of interpreting Scripture — every doctrine proved by at least two or three scriptures before it is accepted as binding — is a later methodological claim. It must be tested, not adopted as if 2 Corinthians 13:1 had already written a hermeneutics manual.

**What the claim means.** A later doctrine that hangs on one isolated usefulness, against the rest of the subject, has not been established as the writings’ communication of that subject.

**What the biblical sentences establish.** Testimony is not established by one witness in the judicial scenes those verses govern. A “word” in 2 Corinthians 13:1 is established in the mouth of two or three witnesses. The analogical step from judicial testimony to doctrinal proof is an inference. It is a sound inference so far as it refuses isolation: a communicating corpus on a subject is not mastered by one clause used against the neighbours. It is an unsound inference if it is treated as a ban on receiving a single clear sentence as a clear sentence. “I am the God of Abraham” is one citation in Matthew 22, and it is decisive as used with the rest of what the scriptures and the power of God require. The Son’s “It is written again” in Matthew 4 is the second writing judging the isolated use of the first.

**What follows for mishandling.** A doctrine out of harmony with any one written statement is already false as a claim to be the writings’ doctrine. “As it is written” remains a guide: any later claim that cannot sit with what is written is already a failed handling. The reconstructible Introduction note that “as it is written” is one of the safest guides to truth and fallacy coheres here: harmony with the written thing is the test; novelty against the written thing is the failure.

**What does not follow here.** That Movement X’s discipline of interpretation has been written. That a concordance-method has been imposed as a second Graphē. That two citations, stacked without sense, become knowledge. Quotation of two clauses can still be wresting. Number of citations is not yet understanding.

Thus:

> **Comparison is a refusal of isolation. A later doctrine that silences neighbours has already misread. One clear sentence remains a clear sentence. A stack of citations is not, by stacking, a true handling.**

---

# 67.36 “As It Is Written” as Guide, Not as a Ban on Sense

The reconstructible Introduction claim that Christ never once gave an interpretation of what was written, or left one to believe that any part of it needed interpretation, and that His application of what was written to certain events was sufficient as to the meaning, must be tested with the same care Chapter 66 already required.

**What can be received.** He treated what was written as already having meaning. He did not treat the writing as empty until a later interpreter filled it. He applied “it is written” as court. He did not grant that the writing says one thing and means another until a school supplies the second meaning. Those sentences cohere with John 10, with Matthew 4, with Matthew 22, and with Luke 24’s exposition in the scriptures.

**What cannot be received as a ban.** Nehemiah 8:8 records giving the sense. Luke 24 records expounding and opening understanding. Acts 8 records beginning at the same scripture and preaching Jesus. Chapter 66 already refused to treat 2 Peter 1:20 as a ban on stating sense. The present file refuses to treat “Christ applied rather than replaced” as “no later mouth may state sense.” Application is sense exhibited. Exposition is sense given. Both sit under the writing.

The guide, then, is this: “as it is written” tests later speech by the written thing. It does not forbid later speech that states what the written thing communicates. Misreading includes treating “as it is written” as a charm that makes any cited clause true as used, and treating “interpretation” as a crime so that the writing is left unused as communication.

Thus:

> **“As it is written” is a guide of later speech by the writing. It is not a baptism of every citation, and it is not a ban on stating the sense the writing communicates.**

---

# 67.37 Reconstructing the Bible-Introduction Proposition: Why the Writing Is Simple and Why It Is Not Understood

A reconstructible proposition from the Bible Introduction materials states that the Bible is simple because it is a revelation, because its truths are repeated, because it is written in the most simple human terms possible, because God is the author and a deity who could not or would not make Himself clear would not be the God who judges by what He has spoken, because it was given to be understood by the simple and trusting, because reading and believing are required, and because the greater part is plain history, promises, and instruction, the rest being prophecy as history written beforehand; and that the Bible is not understood because of reasoning that implies doubt, lack of perception, ignorance, hardness of heart, dull eyes, dull ears, and dull memory — and that these reasons are willful.

The proposition is not adopted as “the source says.” It is tested.

**What is claimed.** The writing is given to be understood. The ordinary failure is not a defect in the Giver or in the writing as communication. The ordinary failure is refused operations of the reader.

**Premises already in force.** Revelation has been given (Chapter 29). Inspiration guarantees a truthful record of what is communicated (Chapters 56–57). The Father’s word is truth (Chapter 64). The Graphē is the primary written authority (Chapter 65). Mark 8, Matthew 13 / Isaiah 6, and John 8:43 have been examined as poor perception. Matthew 22:29 and Luke 24 have been examined as deficient understanding.

**Biblical correspondence.** Mark 8:17–18 names perception, hardness, unused eyes, unused ears, unused memory — the Introduction’s list has a scene. Isaiah 6:9–10 and Matthew 13:13–15 name hearing without understanding and eyes closed. Hebrews 5:11 names dullness of hearing as a condition of hearers, not of a complicated object; the dedicated *apeiros*-file remains later, the correspondence for dullness as a hearer-operation is already available. 2 Timothy 3:15–17 names writings able to make wise unto salvation. Psalm 119:130: “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.”

**What follows.** The proposition coheres with the catalog: the five modes are reader-operations toward a communicating writing. Simplicity of the writing is not the claim that no sentence is hard. 2 Peter 3:16 remains in force. Simplicity is the claim that hardness is not a remaining unintelligible residue that baptizes invention, and that the ordinary closed organs are the reader’s.

**What does not follow here.** That every later difficulty is already hardness of heart. A eunuch may need a guide. That labour has been examined. Diligence remains later. That the writing is a childish book. Simple terms are not thin truth.

Thus:

> **The reconstructible Introduction proposition is received as coherence: the writing is given to be understood; the ordinary reasons it is not understood are refused operations. Hardness of some things remains real. Invention is not thereby licensed.**

---

# 67.38 Reconstructing the Bible-Introduction Proposition: The Literal Rule and the Rejection of Novel Opinion

A second reconstructible proposition from the same materials states the rule observed: take the Bible literally wherein it is at all possible; if symbolic, figurative, or typical language is used, then look for the literal truth it intends to convey; give the same literal meanings to words, and apply the same rules of grammar, figures, types, symbols, allegories, parables, poetry, prophecy, and history, that would be applied if those forms were found outside the Bible; never change the literal meaning to a spiritual, mystical, symbolic, or figurative meaning unless the writing itself does so; prove teachings by plain related passages; lay aside novel interpretations and theories supported by personal opinion alone; and invite the reader to see for himself what the related passages are actually saying.

The proposition is not adopted as “the source says.” It is tested.

**What is claimed.** The writing is to be handled as a communicating book among books, not as a book that says one thing and means another. Figures remain figures and yield a literal truth. Opinion is not the court. Related passages are the court.

**Premises already in force.** The Graphē is a communicating writing (Chapters 56–57, 64–65). Interpretation is accountable sense-giving (Chapter 66). Spiritualizing against communication and missing a figure’s literal truth have already been named as improper handling. Isolation has already been named as context failure.

**Biblical correspondence.** Matthew 22:29 corrects error by what is written, not by a second meaning that evacuates Exodus 3. Matthew 4 answers a cited writing by another writing. Luke 24 expounds in the scriptures. John 2:21 states the literal truth a figure conveyed. Mark 7 judges a later device by Moses’ command as written. Acts 17:11 searches the scriptures whether those things were so.

**What follows.** The rule coheres with the fifth mode: exchanging a communicated sense for a later opinion is improper handling; treating a figure as if it conveyed no literal truth is the same operation from the other side. The invitation to see what related passages say is coherence with comparison, not a second gate.

**What does not follow here.** That every later note printed beside a text is false. Helps remain helps. That a complete hermeneutical manual has been written. Movement X remains the labour-file. That “Christ never interpreted” has been adopted as a ban. That ban was already refused.

Thus:

> **The reconstructible literal rule is received as coherence with communicating writing: the sense is the writing’s; figures yield their literal truth; novel opinion is not the court. The labour-file remains later.**

---

# 67.39 Reconstructing the Aletheia Proposition: Analogical Religiousism as a Mode of Misreading

A reconstructible proposition from the project’s own doctrinal materials states that true experience in conformity with Christ pillows in the unleavened sincerity and truth of the Graphē — Holy Writ as writings of unchallenged standing — and that the ersatz analogue is analogical, nonliteral religiousism: a later likeness that will not sit under the writing, whether in a person or in a house.

The proposition is not adopted as “the source says.” It is tested.

**What is claimed.** Experience that is truly in conformity with Christ takes its measure from the Graphē’s truth. A substitute that uses the writing as a likeness to bless a later invention is already a failed handling. “Nonliteral” here names that substitute, not the existence of figures in the writings.

**Premises.** The Graphē is the primary written authority (Chapter 65). A later claim about the writing is not the writing (Chapter 66). Improper handling includes exchanging the communicated sense for a second sense the writing does not give.

**Biblical correspondence.** John 8:31–32: continue in His word; know the truth; the truth makes free. John 10:35: the scripture cannot be broken. Mark 7:13: the word made of none effect. 2 Peter 3:16: wresting. Matthew 15:9: teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.

**What follows.** Analogical religiousism, controlled as a later likeness that will not sit under the writing, is a mode of misreading: the writing is used as decoration of a later invention. The invention may be personal or organizational. Size does not create a new mode.

**What does not follow here.** That figures, types, and parables have been denied. They remain in the writings. That every later practice calling itself Christian has been examined as a heresy. The heresy-file remains later. That First Principles have been taught because “unleavened sincerity and truth” has been named.

Thus:

> **The reconstructible Aletheia proposition is received as coherence: a later likeness that will not sit under the Graphē is already a misreading. Figures in the writings are not that likeness. The heresy-file remains later.**

---

# 67.40 Reconstructing the Aletheia Proposition: Absence of Sound Judgment as the Handling Failure

A second reconstructible proposition from the same materials states that the absence of reasonability — sound judgment — and the presence of unskillfulness are responsible for later aridity, tergiversation, and accepted heresies among persons and organizations that claim the name; that this lack of skill is blamed on failure to realize the scholarly impetus of the scripture; and that anyone unskilled in the word of righteousness is named a babe.

The proposition is not adopted as “the source says.” It is tested.

**What is claimed.** Failed judgment and failed skill in the word are causes of later turning aside and of later accepted error. The writing’s intellectual demand is not optional.

**What may be used now.** Sound judgment is already a defined operation (Chapter 6). Isaiah 1:18 is already an invitation to reason (Chapter 7). The five modes are already operations of failed judgment toward a writing. Absence of sound judgment is therefore already visible as the join of those modes: a reader who will not perceive, will not grasp, infers falsely, isolates, and handles improperly has already refused reasonability toward the writing.

**What may not be used as finished.** Aridity as a dedicated file (Chapter 72). Tergiversation as a dedicated file (Chapter 70). Accepted heresies as a dedicated file (Chapter 71). *Apeiros* and the babe as dedicated files (Chapters 73 and 81). Scholarly impetus and *spoudazō* as dedicated files (Chapters 74 and 78). The First Principles as content. The proposition’s causal chain is named as neighbourhood. Neighbourhood is not arrival.

**Biblical correspondence available now.** Mark 8 joins reasoning, perception, and hardness. Matthew 22:29 joins error and not-knowing. 2 Peter 3:16 joins unlearned instability and wresting. Hebrews 5:11–13 names dull hearing and unskillfulness as conditions of hearers who ought to be teachers; those verses may be cited as correspondence that failed hearing and failed skill are real. They may not be used as if the dedicated files had been written.

Thus:

> **The reconstructible causal chain is received only as coherence with the modes: refused sound judgment toward the writing is already misreading. The later pathology-files and labour-files remain later.**

# 67.41 The Ten Classes Reconstructed as Modes, Not as a Psychology of Blame

A reconstructible list from the Bible Introduction materials names ten classes who find the Bible hard to understand: those ignorant of its contents; those too lazy to read it; those biased contrary to its true doctrines; rebels who have listened to teachers who explain it away; those uninterested because of the theory that it is hard to understand; those too worldly and sinful to believe it because it condemns them; unstable souls who wrest to their own destruction; deceivers who use it to further their own interests; those whom Satan blinds and robs of truth; those who refuse to humble themselves and be converted.

The list is not adopted as a finished psychology, and it is not adopted as “the source says.” It is tested as a classification of operations already named.

**Ignorance of contents** is poor perception and deficient understanding in their most ordinary form: the writing has not been taken in. **Laziness toward reading** is refused intake. **Bias contrary to the doctrines** is already a decided heart: Matthew 13’s closed eyes. **Listening to teachers who explain it away** is receiving a later handling that evacuates — Mark 7’s field occupied, force removed — without yet writing the teacher as a system. **The theory that it is hard** is despair’s popular form, already refused as a fallacy in Chapter 66 and now named as a cause of refused labour toward a communicating writing. **Refusal because the writing condemns** is John 3:20’s neighbourhood: he that doeth evil hateth the light. **Unstable wresting** is 2 Peter 3:16. **Use to further interests** is 2 Corinthians 2:17 and 4:2. **Blindness** is 2 Corinthians 4:4 and Matthew 13:19. **Refusal to be converted** is Isaiah 6:10’s “lest they be converted.”

**What follows.** The ten classes, controlled as operations, map onto the five modes. They do not add an eleventh mode called “personality.” They exhibit that the same operations have several faces.

**What does not follow here.** That every later difficulty is already one of the ten as a completed moral verdict. The eunuch is not in the ten as a wrestler. That Satanology has been written as a system. Blindness is named. The system is not. That conversion has been examined as a First Principle.

Thus:

> **The reconstructible ten classes are received as faces of the five modes, not as a second catalog and not as a finished psychology. Difficulty remains distinguishable from wresting.**

---

# 67.42 Competing Claim: The Bible Is Inherently Obscure, Therefore Misreading Is the Text’s Fault

The reduction says:

> **Readers fail. Therefore the writing is obscure. Misreading is the text’s fault. To examine modes of the reader is to blame the hearer for a sealed book. Difficulty in 2 Peter 3:16 is the whole truth about the corpus.**

The reduction fails.

The premise that some things are hard to be understood is granted. 2 Peter 3:16 states it. The conclusion that the writing is a sealed book whose failures are its own is not granted. The same verse names wresting of writings that stand, and names destruction as the handlers’. Hardness and wresting are two. Chapter 66 already refused despair: fallibility of the reader does not migrate into the writing. The present file uses that refusal: obscurity-as-fault-of-the-text is despair applied to the catalog.

The biblical record refuses the reduction in several mouths at once. Psalm 119:130 assigns light and understanding to the entrance of the words, including to the simple. Deuteronomy 29:29 assigns revealed things to Israel and to their children, that they may do them. Matthew 11:25 records things hid from the wise and prudent and revealed unto babes — not hid in the writing as a defect, but hid from a kind of hearer. Luke 24 records writings that already spoke, and understanding opened toward them. Acts 8 records a writing that could be begun at and preached. 2 Timothy 3:15–17 records writings able to make wise unto salvation and profitable for doctrine, reproof, correction, and instruction. Those sentences are unintelligible if the corpus is a sealed charm.

The reduction often presents itself as humility before mystery. The humility is a claim of immunity. If the writing is at fault, the reader is safe from the modes. Safety from the modes is not reverence. It is the later act refusing to appear as an act.

Thus:

> **“The writing is obscure, therefore misreading is the text’s fault” fails. Hardness of some things is affirmed. Fault of the corpus as corpus is denied. The modes remain the reader’s operations.**

---

# 67.43 Competing Claim: Every Sincere Reading Is a Valid Reading

The reduction says:

> **The reader is sincere. Therefore the reading is valid. To name misreading is to judge the heart. Sincerity baptizes sense.**

The reduction fails.

Chapters 1–3 already established that sincerity is not a determinant of truth. Chapter 66 already established that a later claim about the writing is still a claim. The present file uses both: sincerity is a manner of the speaker; correspondence is a relation of the claim to the writing. A sincere miss is still a miss. An insincere hit, if a man happened to state what the writing communicates while intending something else, would still be measured by the writing, not by the intention — though the writings also name deceitful handling as a crime of manner. Manner and correspondence are two.

The biblical record refuses the reduction. The Sadducees’ question may have been a sincere party-puzzle. It is still named as error. The disciples’ bread-inference may have been sincere worry. It is still named as failure to understand. The woman’s added “neither shall ye touch it” may have been sincere caution. It is still a distortion of the given wording. 2 Corinthians 2:17 contrasts sincerity with corrupting the word: sincerity there is refused mixture, not a baptism of every mixed reading that feels honest.

The reduction often presents itself as charity. Charity that abolishes the court is not charity toward the hearer. It leaves the hearer with a sincere miss and no measure.

Thus:

> **“Every sincere reading is a valid reading” fails. Sincerity is not correspondence. A sincere miss remains a misreading. The writing remains the court.**

---

# 67.44 Competing Claim: Spiritualizing Is the Higher Method

The reduction says:

> **The letter is for the simple. The higher method is to treat statements of fact and history as vehicles of a later spiritual sense that need not leave the stated thing standing. To refuse this is naivety. Christ Himself used figures; therefore the corpus is a figure.**

The reduction fails.

The existence of figures is granted. Parables, symbols, types, and figures are in the writings. John 2:19, Matthew 16:6, and the parables of Matthew 13 are enough. The conclusion that therefore statements of fact and history may be exchanged for a later sense that evacuates them is not granted. That exchange is the first abuse already named: spiritualizing against the communication.

The writings refuse the exchange as a method. Luke 24 treats Moses, the prophets, and the psalms as writings that already spoke of Christ’s sufferings and glory — not as a code that leaves the sufferings unasserted. Matthew 22 treats Exodus 3 as a statement whose force toward living patriarchs stands. Mark 7 treats “Honour thy father and thy mother” as a command that still commands. John 10 treats “I said, Ye are gods” as wording that still words. A method that would have those sentences mean something else that leaves the stated thing unasserted has already misread them.

Christ’s use of figures does not convert the corpus into a figure. He distinguishes parable and explanation (Matthew 13). He distinguishes “this temple” as body from the hearers’ building-inference (John 2). He reasons from the letter of Psalm 82 (Chapters 59–61, used not retried). Figure is a form the writings use. Figure is not a licence to evacuate.

The reduction often presents itself as depth. Depth that will not sit under what is written is not depth. It is a later invention using the writing as decoration. Analogical religiousism, already tested, is this reduction’s popular form.

Thus:

> **“Spiritualizing is the higher method” fails. Figures are granted. Evacuation of communicated fact, command, promise, or history is refused. Figure is a form, not a licence.**

---

# 67.45 Competing Claim: One Useful Verse Suffices

The reduction says:

> **I have a verse. The verse is useful. Therefore the doctrine is established. Comparison is obstruction. Neighbours are optional. “The Bible says” means “this clause serves.”**

The reduction fails.

A clear sentence remains a clear sentence. The reduction’s error is not that one sentence can communicate. Matthew 22’s citation is one sentence, decisive as used. The error is usefulness as the test, and isolation as the method. Usefulness is not correspondence. A clause can serve a later interest and fail of the writing. 2 Corinthians 2:17 already named that use. Matthew 4 already exhibited a useful citation in a later mouth.

The writings refuse usefulness as court. Isaiah 8:20 sends a people to the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, there is no light in them. The test is according to the word, not according to service of a later aim. Galatians 1:8–9 measures a later gospel by the deposit already received, not by the later gospel’s usefulness. Mark 7’s Corban was useful to a later device. It made the word of none effect.

Comparison, already tested, refuses the method without becoming a stack-of-citations charm. Neighbours govern force. A doctrine out of harmony with any one written statement is already false as a claim to be the writings’ doctrine. “As it is written” remains the guide.

Thus:

> **“One useful verse suffices” fails. A clear sentence can communicate. Usefulness is not the court. Isolation is already context failure. A later interest is already improper handling when it governs the clause.**

---

# 67.46 Competing Claim: This Chapter as Already Chapters 68–73 or Movement X

The reduction says:

> **Once the modes have been named, the systems have been examined, the displacement has been traced, the pathologies have been written, and the labour has been performed. The later chapters are surplus.**

The reduction fails.

The locked TOC distinguishes the assignments in distinct sentences. This chapter examines errors arising from poor perception, deficient understanding, faulty inference, context failure, or improper handling of the text. Chapter 68 examines theology, philosophy, tradition, and institution as systems. Chapter 69 examines secondary sources becoming primary. Chapters 70–73 examine tergiversation, accepted heresies, aridity, and *apeiros*. Movement X examines scholarly labour, *spoudazō*, rightly dividing, and readiness for the First Principles. Distinction of assignments is not a delay of nerve. It is the knowledge-flow the book has followed from Chapter 1.

A pious form of collapse says: the rest is obvious, so write it now. Obviousness is not architecture. The modes are premises of later files. A premise is not those files under another name. Chapter 66 already refused the collapse when it was offered as “the distinction is already the catalog.” This chapter refuses the remaining half: the catalog is not already the systems, the displacement, the pathologies, or the labour.

Mark 7 has been used as handling that evacuates. Evacuation exhibited is not tradition examined as a system. Hebrews 5:11–13 has been used as correspondence that dull hearing and unskillfulness are real. Correspondence is not the *apeiros*-file. *Spoudazō* has been named as later. Naming is not performing.

Thus:

> **This chapter is not already Chapters 68–73 or Movement X. The modes are the modes. Later questions remain later.**

# 67.47 Reason Through the Evidence

The inference can now be exhibited.

**Premise 1.** The Graphē is the primary written authority by which truth is known, tested, reasoned through, taught, discerned, and lived (Chapter 65, used not retried).

**Premise 2.** The authority of that writing is distinct from the authority claimed for a later statement of sense. The writing’s standing does not transfer. Fallibility of the reader is compatible with infallibility of the record. An authoritative truthful text does not make every interpretation authoritative. The fact that readers err does not make all readings equal (Chapter 66, used not retried).

**Premise 3.** The record does not fail as truthful divine writing of what it actually communicates (Chapter 57, used not retried). A communicating writing can be received and can be failed of.

**Premise 4.** The writings themselves diagnose failed later acts as operations: unused eyes and ears (Mark 8; Matthew 13 / Isaiah 6); speech not understood because the word is not heard (John 8:43); not knowing the scriptures while handling them (Matthew 22:29); reading without grasp (Acts 8); slowness toward writings that already speak (Luke 24); reasoning from a genuine sentence to the wrong object (Matthew 16); a wrong referent attached to a genuine sentence (John 2); a genuine citation used for an invalid step (Matthew 4); distortion of a given wording (Genesis 3); wresting of writings that stand (2 Peter 3:16); corrupting and deceitful handling (2 Corinthians 2:17; 4:2); making the word of none effect (Mark 7 / Matthew 15).

**Premise 5.** Those operations are classifiable, without remainder of the locked assignment, as poor perception, deficient understanding, faulty inference, context failure, and improper handling. The five may combine. They remain distinguishable.

**Premise 6.** Reconstructible Introduction and Aletheia propositions, tested rather than cited as authority, cohere: the writing is given to be understood; ordinary failure is refused operations; the literal communication is not to be exchanged for novel opinion; a later likeness that will not sit under the Graphē is already a misreading; absence of sound judgment is already visible as the join of the modes. Later pathology-files and labour-files remain later.

**Premise 7.** Competing reductions fail: fault of the text as corpus; sincerity as baptism; spiritualizing as higher method; usefulness of one isolated clause as court; this file as already Chapters 68–73 or Movement X.

**Inference.** Therefore Scripture is misread when the later act of stating sense fails to correspond to what the writing actually communicates, and that failure occurs in the five named modes. The writing remains the measure of the failure. A correct reading remains possible. An incorrect reading remains incorrect. The catalog is warranted at this level and not beyond it.

The inference is not a leap from “readers can err” to “these five names.” The five names are the locked assignment’s species, filled by the writings’ own diagnoses and tested against the reconstructible source-propositions. The inference is not a leap from “modes exist” to “systems have been examined.” Sequence forbids that leap.

Thus:

> **The join is inspectable: ranked writing + distinguished later act + communicating record + the writings’ own diagnoses + five named operations + refused reductions = a warranted catalog of how Scripture is misread, at this level and not beyond it.**

# 67.48 Explicit Versus Inferred

What is explicit in the writings used here includes: unused eyes and ears, hardness, unused memory (Mark 8); seeing without seeing and hearing without hearing (Matthew 13; Isaiah 6); speech not understood because the word is not heard (John 8:43); “ye do err, not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of God” (Matthew 22:29); “Understandest thou what thou readest?” (Acts 8:30); slowness of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken, and understanding opened toward the scriptures (Luke 24); a warning about leaven taken as a sentence about bread (Matthew 16); “this temple” taken as a building (John 2); “it is written” used to urge a leap, answered by “it is written again” (Matthew 4); a given command questioned, added to, softened, and reversed (Genesis 3); things hard to be understood, wrested by the unlearned and unstable unto their own destruction (2 Peter 3:16); corrupting the word; handling the word deceitfully (2 Corinthians 2:17; 4:2); making the word of God of none effect through tradition (Mark 7:13).

What is inferred, and warranted by the join, is that these explicit operations are the modes the locked assignment names — poor perception, deficient understanding, faulty inference, context failure, improper handling — and that “how Scripture is misread” is this catalog rather than a mood, a fate, or a fault of the corpus as corpus.

What is not inferred here: that theology, philosophy, tradition, and institution have been examined as systems; that secondary sources becoming primary has been traced as a finished displacement; that tergiversation, accepted heresies, aridity, or *apeiros* have been written as dedicated files; that *spoudazō*, rightly dividing, or the First Principles have been established; that every later difficulty is already hardness of heart; that stating sense is forbidden; that figures do not exist; that one clear sentence cannot communicate.

The distinction between explicit and inferred is itself part of the chapter’s honesty. The writings name operations. The catalog names those operations as the five modes. The later files remain later.

Thus:

> **What the writings name as failed operations is explicit. That those operations are this chapter’s five modes is the warranted inference. Later doctrines have not been inferred here.**

# 67.49 The Warranted Conclusion Stated with Full Force

The conclusion may now be stated without postponement and without inflation.

Scripture is misread when the later act of stating the Graphē’s sense fails to correspond to what that writing actually communicates. That failure is not a fate, not a mystery of a sealed book, and not a single fog called “error.” It is a set of inspectable operations.

**Poor perception** refuses or neglects the intake of what the writing presents: eyes that do not see, ears that do not hear, memory that does not serve, a word that is not heard.

**Deficient understanding** fails to grasp the sense of a writing that communicates: words in hand, the scriptures not known; a reading without grasp; slowness toward writings that already speak.

**Faulty inference** draws from a genuine sentence a conclusion the communication does not warrant: the wrong object, the wrong referent, an invalid step from a true citation.

**Context failure** refuses the writing’s own placement of a sentence among its neighbours: isolation; distortion of given wording; ignoring speaker, audience, occasion, or scope.

**Improper handling** uses the writing against its own communication: wresting, corrupting, deceitful use, making the word of none effect, exchanging the communicated sense for a second sense the writing does not give, or using the writing to further a later interest.

The writing remains the measure of those operations. Wresting does not unmake standing. Isolation does not rewrite neighbours. A sincere miss remains a miss. A useful clause remains a clause. A figure remains a figure that conveys a literal truth. A recorded lie remains a recorded lie.

A correct reading remains possible because the writing communicates. An incorrect reading remains incorrect because the writing communicates. Transfer remains invalid. Despair remains invalid. The catalog does not baptize the reader. The catalog does not abolish knowledge.

This continues Movement IX. It is not Chapter 66 retried. It is not Chapters 68–73. It is not Movement X. That is this chapter’s conclusion, stated here with full force.

Thus:

> **How Scripture is misread has been examined as five operations of a later act toward a standing, communicating writing. The catalog is in force. Later questions remain later because they are different questions.**

---

# 67.50 Apply the Standard

The standard has been applied.

A later claim about the Graphē is now to be asked not only, “Is this the writing, or a later statement of sense?” — Chapter 66’s question — but, “By which operation, if any, does this later statement fail of the writing?” Does it fail at intake? At grasp? At the step? At the neighbours? At the use?

The questions are practical without becoming a manual. A people who possess copies may still not perceive what is on the page. A people who can quote may still not know the scriptures they quote. A people who reason may still reason to the wrong object. A people who have a verse may still have isolated it. A people who occupy the field of the word may still have made the word of none effect.

The standard also protects. Difficulty is not already wresting. Disagreement is not already proof that every party has misread. A figure is not already a licence, and a literal sentence is not already a naivety. A guide who begins at the same scripture is not already a second Graphē. An office, a tradition, a commentary, or a school may serve. Service is not this chapter’s denial. This chapter denies only the failed operations, and it leaves the later files to examine those speakers as systems and as displacements.

The standard is the writing. The operations are the later act. The catalog is the join.

Thus:

> **The standard has been applied: how Scripture is misread has been examined as Movement IX’s second word, not announced as a slogan, and not postponed as if the modes were weak.**

---

# 67.51 From Modes of Misreading to Systems Beside the Graphē

A catalog, now controlled as five operations of a later act, still leaves a further question.

The species-file is in force. Scripture is misread by poor perception, deficient understanding, faulty inference, context failure, and improper handling. The writing remains the measure. Those sentences are the cleared ground. They are not yet the dedicated examination of secondary intellectual and institutional systems in relation to the Graphē: theology, philosophy, tradition, and institution, none of which becomes primary authority merely by claiming Christian identity, academic status, antiquity, or institutional recognition.

If the modes were not named, the next question would still be how Scripture is misread. The modes have been named. If this chapter were already that later examination, the next file would be repetition. This chapter is not that later examination. The next question is therefore the construction the locked assignment names: Theology, Philosophy, Tradition, and Institution.

That is the proper open of the next chapter. The catalog was never meant to be a slogan that finishes Movement IX, and it was never meant to baptize every later system or to treat every later system as already one of the five modes under another name. It was meant to be the naming of the operations by which the later act fails, sufficient to justify taking the next question, which is the question those operations themselves force once they have been named in persons: what are the secondary systems that stand beside the Graphē, and how do they stand toward it?

The next file must not steal this catalog as if modes had not been named. This file must not steal that system-file as if Chapter 68 were already written. Naming the neighbourhood is not performing the examination.

---

# What Has Been Established

This chapter has established:

1. **How Scripture is misread, in this argument, is the dedicated catalog of the later act failing to correspond to what the Graphē actually communicates, examined as inspectable modes — not a mood, not a second distinction, and not the later files.**
2. **Misreading at this stage is failed correspondence of a later statement of sense to the writing’s communication — not mere difficulty, not mere disagreement, not the writing’s collapse.**
3. **The five modes are operations: poor perception (intake), deficient understanding (grasp), faulty inference (invalid step), context failure (refused placement), improper handling (use against the communication).**
4. **Modes matter because failure is operational, not mystical and not fate.**
5. **Positive warrant, first member: the writing communicates; failure is the later act, not the writing’s silence.**
6. **Positive warrant, second member: the writings themselves diagnose the operations.**
7. **Positive warrant, third member: a correct reading remains possible; the catalog does not abolish knowledge.**
8. **Mark 8:17–18 warrants poor perception as unused eyes, ears, and memory toward a sentence in the ear.**
9. **Matthew 13:13–15 and Isaiah 6:9–10 warrant seeing without seeing and hearing without hearing.**
10. **John 8:43 warrants speech not understood because the word is not heard.**
11. **Matthew 22:29 warrants deficient understanding as not knowing the scriptures while handling them.**
12. **Acts 8:30–35 warrants reading without grasp, and help as sense given from the same writing.**
13. **Luke 24:25–27, 44–45 warrant slowness toward writings that already speak, and understanding opened toward those writings.**
14. **Matthew 16:6–12 warrants faulty inference as reasoning from a genuine sentence to the wrong object.**
15. **John 2:19–22 warrants a wrong referent attached to a genuine sentence, and the literal truth a figure conveyed.**
16. **Matthew 4:5–7 warrants a genuine citation used for an invalid step, judged by another writing.**
17. **Genesis 3:1–5 warrants distortion of a given wording: questioning, adding, softening, reversing.**
18. **Isolation of a true clause from its neighbours is already a false use when the neighbours govern the force.**
19. **Speaker, audience, occasion, and scope are neighbours; ignoring them is already context failure.**
20. **2 Peter 3:16 warrants wresting of writings that stand, including hard things; hardness is not the wresting.**
21. **2 Corinthians 2:17 and 4:2 warrant corrupting and deceitful handling of the word.**
22. **Mark 7 and Matthew 15 warrant making the word of none effect while occupying the field of the word; the system-file remains later.**
23. **Improper handling includes exchanging the communicated sense for a second sense the writing does not give, whether by spiritualizing away what is said or by missing the literal truth a figure conveys.**
24. **Speaker-distinction is a handling-rule: presence in the writing is not endorsement of every speaker.**
25. **Comparison refuses isolation; a stack of citations is not, by stacking, a true handling; one clear sentence remains a clear sentence.**
26. **“As it is written” is a guide of later speech by the writing, not a baptism of every citation and not a ban on stating sense.**
27. **The reconstructible Introduction proposition that the writing is given to be understood, and that ordinary failure is refused operations, is received as coherence.**
28. **The reconstructible literal rule and the rejection of novel opinion are received as coherence with communicating writing.**
29. **The reconstructible Aletheia proposition that a later likeness which will not sit under the Graphē is already a misreading is received as coherence; figures in the writings are not that likeness.**
30. **The reconstructible causal chain from refused sound judgment to later pathologies is named as neighbourhood, not as Chapters 70–73 or Movement X.**
31. **The reconstructible ten classes are faces of the five modes, not a second catalog.**
32. **“The writing is obscure, therefore misreading is the text’s fault” fails.**
33. **“Every sincere reading is a valid reading” fails.**
34. **“Spiritualizing is the higher method” fails.**
35. **“One useful verse suffices” fails.**
36. **Treating this chapter as already Chapters 68–73 or Movement X fails.**
37. **What is explicit has been distinguished from what is inferred, and later doctrines have not been inferred here.**
38. **The catalog attaches to operations of the later act. It does not confer the writing’s standing upon every later quotation, tradition, impression, institution, or reader.**
39. **This chapter continues Movement IX because its assigned word has been stated.**
40. **This chapter opens Chapter 68 by naming the next necessary question without answering it.**
41. **What is reserved is Chapters 68–73; entire Movement X (Chapters 74–85); the First Principles themselves; and σπουδάζω (*spoudazō*) as a dedicated chapter.**

---

# Chapter Summary

> **The chapter’s central conclusion:** Scripture is misread when the later act of stating sense fails to correspond to what the Graphē actually communicates. Because the writing is the primary written authority already earned; because that authority has been distinguished from the authority claimed for a later statement of sense; because the record does not fail as truthful divine writing of what it actually communicates; and because the writings themselves diagnose unused perception, not-knowing, invalid steps, isolation and distortion of wording, and wresting, corrupting, deceitful, and evacuating use — the failure is inspectable as poor perception, deficient understanding, faulty inference, context failure, and improper handling. The writing remains the measure. A correct reading remains possible. An incorrect reading remains incorrect. Competing reductions fail: fault of the text as corpus; sincerity as baptism; spiritualizing as higher method; usefulness of one isolated clause as court; this chapter as already Chapters 68–73 or Movement X.
